PLX-BCH-008.detail: Vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed with dietary lipid in micelles and carried in chylomicrons, so they become deficient in fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, cholestasis). They are stored in tissue and can accumulate to toxic levels, unlike most water-soluble vitamins. Vitamin D can also be made in skin and vitamin K by gut bacteria, but dietary uptake of both still requires fat absorption.
tileNotes: Retinol is vitamin A, needed for rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors and for epithelial differentiation.
Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3, made in skin with UV light or absorbed from the diet, then hydroxylated in liver and kidney.
Tocopherol is vitamin E, a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation.
Phylloquinone is vitamin K1, the plant form of vitamin K required for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.

GI-033.detail: All four are inherited defects in how the liver processes bilirubin, but they fall into two pairs. Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar reduce conjugation by UGT1A1 and cause unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. Dubin-Johnson and Rotor impair storage or excretion of already conjugated bilirubin and cause conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia. They differ from acquired causes such as hemolysis, hepatitis, or biliary obstruction, and not all are benign: Crigler-Najjar type I can cause kernicterus.
tileNotes: Mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity, usually from a promoter variant, causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Jaundice appears with fasting, stress, illness, or exertion, and liver tests are otherwise normal.

UGT1A1 activity is absent in type I or severely reduced in type II, causing marked unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Type I presents in newborns, risks kernicterus, and needs phototherapy or liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital.
A defect in MRP2 (ABCC2), the canalicular pump, blocks excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile, causing benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Retained pigment makes the liver grossly black.
Impaired hepatic uptake and storage of conjugated bilirubin causes mild, benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It resembles Dubin-Johnson but is milder and the liver is not black.

Defective excretion (MRP2) → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; grossly black liver.
Defective hepatic storage/excretion → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; liver NOT black.

MSK-001.detail: The rotator cuff is the four muscles remembered as SITS that run from the scapula to the humeral head and hold it in the shallow glenoid while the arm moves. Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle, and subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Teres major, deltoid, and latissimus dorsi also move the shoulder but are not cuff muscles because they do not form this stabilizing sleeve around the joint capsule.
tileNotes: Runs above the scapular spine to the greater tubercle and initiates abduction for about the first 15 degrees. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve, it is the most commonly impinged and torn cuff muscle (empty can test).
Sits below the scapular spine and inserts on the greater tubercle, where it is the main external rotator of the arm. It is innervated by the suprascapular nerve and is often injured in pitchers.

A small muscle along the lateral scapular border that inserts on the greater tubercle and externally rotates and adducts the arm. It is innervated by the axillary nerve, unlike its look-alike teres major, which is not a cuff muscle.
The only cuff muscle on the anterior scapula, inserting on the lesser tubercle to internally rotate and adduct the arm. It is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

tileNotes: Abducts the arm (first ~15°); most commonly torn and impinged.
Externally rotates the arm.
Externally rotates and adducts the arm.
Internally rotates the arm; the only one on the anterior scapula.

NEU-052.detail: These are the cardinal motor signs of Parkinson disease (TRAP), caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies. Bradykinesia is required for diagnosis, plus rest tremor or rigidity, and postural instability usually comes later. The tremor occurs at rest, unlike the action tremor of essential tremor or the intention tremor of cerebellar disease. Prominent falls early in the course suggest atypical parkinsonism such as progressive supranuclear palsy.
tileNotes: Slowness and progressive decrease in size and speed of movement, seen as small handwriting, reduced facial expression, and a shuffling gait. It is the core required feature and reflects reduced dopamine in the basal ganglia.
A 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling tremor, usually starting on one side, that is present at rest and lessens with voluntary movement. It may be absent in the akinetic-rigid form of the disease.

Increased tone through the full range of passive movement with a ratchet-like catch, classically explained as rest tremor superimposed on rigidity. It is not velocity-dependent, unlike the spasticity of upper motor neuron lesions.
Loss of postural reflexes that leads to falls and a stooped, festinating gait. It usually appears later in Parkinson disease, so early falls suggest another parkinsonian syndrome.

PSY-006.detail: Positive symptoms are experiences added to normal function: false beliefs, false perceptions, and disorganized speech or behavior. Negative symptoms are losses of normal function, such as flat affect, alogia, avolition, and anhedonia. Schizophrenia requires at least two core symptoms for one month, one of them delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, with six months of disturbance. These positive symptoms are not specific to schizophrenia and also occur in brief psychotic, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, and substance-induced psychotic disorders.
tileNotes: Fixed false beliefs held despite clear contrary evidence and not explained by culture, such as persecutory or referential ideas. They add a belief that should not be there, making them a positive symptom.
Perceptions without an external stimulus, most often auditory voices in schizophrenia. Visual or tactile hallucinations raise concern for substance use or a medical cause.
Speech that reflects disordered thinking, such as derailment, tangentiality, or incoherent word salad. It is one of the three symptoms at least one of which must be present for schizophrenia.

Grossly disorganized behavior, such as unpredictable agitation, bizarre dress or actions, or purposeless activity. It reflects added abnormal behavior rather than the loss of drive seen in negative symptoms.

PULM-001.detail: Drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive spirometry and reduced DLCO. Bleomycin and busulfan are antineoplastic agents, amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic and nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic. Methotrexate and carmustine are also associated with lung toxicity, though methotrexate mainly causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Pulmonary function testing is used to monitor at-risk patients.
tileNotes: Bleomycin generates free radicals that damage lung tissue, which has little bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates the drug elsewhere. Pulmonary fibrosis is its dose-limiting toxicity.
Amiodarone, an iodine-rich antiarrhythmic, accumulates in lung tissue and can cause interstitial pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis. Patients need baseline and follow-up pulmonary function tests.
Long-term nitrofurantoin use, typically for urinary tract infection prophylaxis, can cause chronic interstitial pneumonitis and fibrosis.
Busulfan, an alkylating agent used in conditioning before stem cell transplant, can cause pulmonary fibrosis ('busulfan lung').

tileNotes: A chemotherapy agent with dose-related pulmonary toxicity.
An antiarrhythmic that can cause pulmonary (and hepatic/thyroid) toxicity.
An antimetabolite associated with pneumonitis and fibrosis.
An alkylating agent causing pulmonary fibrosis.

CARD-052.detail: During dynamic (aerobic) exercise such as running or cycling, sympathetic activation raises heart rate and contractility, while the skeletal muscle pump and venoconstriction increase venous return. At the same time, metabolic vasodilation in working muscle lowers systemic vascular resistance, so cardiac output rises substantially. This pattern applies to dynamic exercise and does not generalize to sustained isometric exercise.
tileNotes: Heart rate is the number of beats per minute. In dynamic exercise it rises through reduced vagal tone and increased sympathetic stimulation of the SA node, a major contributor to the rise in cardiac output.
Contractility is the intrinsic strength of myocardial contraction independent of preload and afterload. Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation increases it during dynamic exercise, raising stroke volume.

Venous return is the flow of blood back to the right heart. Rhythmic contraction of exercising muscles squeezes veins (the muscle pump), and sympathetic venoconstriction helps, so more blood returns to fill the heart.

Systemic vascular resistance is the total resistance of the systemic arterioles to flow. In dynamic exercise, local metabolites dilate arterioles in active skeletal muscle, which lowers overall resistance despite sympathetic constriction elsewhere.

PLX-HEM-016.detail: Koilonychia, pica, atrophic glossitis and Plummer-Vinson syndrome are recognized clinical clues to iron deficiency, although none must be present and many patients have only fatigue or pallor. Some are not specific: glossitis also occurs in vitamin B12 and folate deficiency. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a syndrome that includes iron deficiency rather than a single sign of it.
tileNotes: Koilonychia means thin, concave, spoon-shaped nails that can hold a drop of water. It is a classic, though uncommon, sign of chronic iron deficiency.
Pica is a craving to eat non-food substances such as ice (pagophagia), clay or starch. Ice craving in particular is a classic, though not universal, clue to iron deficiency.
Atrophic glossitis is a smooth, red, often sore tongue caused by loss of the papillae. It can be seen in iron deficiency but is shared with vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, so it is not specific.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is the combination of iron deficiency anemia, upper esophageal webs and dysphagia. It contains iron deficiency as one of its components and is associated with an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

GI-009.detail: Obesity, pregnancy, sliding hiatal hernia and scleroderma all predispose to gastroesophageal reflux disease, but through different mechanisms rather than one shared effect on the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). Obesity and pregnancy raise intra-abdominal pressure, a sliding hiatal hernia disrupts the gastroesophageal junction barrier, and scleroderma lowers LES tone and impairs esophageal motility.
tileNotes: Obesity, especially central adiposity, increases intra-abdominal pressure. This pushes gastric contents against the gastroesophageal junction and favors reflux.
Pregnancy raises intra-abdominal pressure as the uterus enlarges. Heartburn is a very common complaint, particularly later in pregnancy.

A sliding hiatal hernia is displacement of the gastroesophageal junction and upper stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the chest. Loss of the normal diaphragmatic support weakens the antireflux barrier.
Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) causes smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the lower esophagus. The result is low LES tone and weak peristalsis, so refluxed acid is poorly cleared.

IMM-026.detail: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome is caused by STAT3 mutations that block Th17 differentiation, reducing IL-17 and neutrophil recruitment. Features are remembered as FATED: coarse Facies, cold (noninflamed) staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, very high IgE, and Dermatologic problems such as eczema. Recurrent lung infections and fractures from minor trauma are also common. DOCK8 deficiency also causes high IgE and eczema but is autosomal recessive with severe viral skin infections and lacks the dental and skeletal features.
tileNotes: Primary teeth fail to shed, so two rows of teeth may be present; a classic connective tissue feature of STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome.
Recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses with little warmth or redness because neutrophil recruitment is impaired.
A chronic eczematous dermatitis that often starts in the newborn period.
Serum IgE is markedly elevated, often above 2,000 IU/mL.

check.by: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
check.note: Retained primary teeth is a FATED feature of STAT3 hyper-IgE and replaces the tile that repeated the title.

history.detail: STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) is an autosomal dominant loss-of-function disorder that impairs Th17 cell development and neutrophil recruitment. It classically presents with eczema, markedly elevated IgE and recurrent staphylococcal abscesses that show little warmth or redness. It should be distinguished from DOCK8 deficiency, and cold abscesses are characteristic but not mandatory.
tileNotes: STAT3 is a signaling protein downstream of several cytokine receptors. Dominant loss-of-function mutations impair Th17 differentiation and IL-17 production, weakening neutrophil-mediated defense of the skin and lungs.

Cold abscesses are collections of pus, often due to Staphylococcus aureus, that lack the usual warmth, redness and pain. They are characteristic of STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome, though not present in every patient.
Eczema is an itchy, inflamed, scaly rash. In STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome it often begins early in life and can become secondarily infected.
Serum IgE is typically very high in this syndrome, often far above levels seen in ordinary atopy. The elevation is a defining laboratory clue but is not specific on its own.

DERM-007.detail: Primary varicella-zoster virus infection is chickenpox. The virus becomes latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and can reactivate as shingles in a dermatomal distribution. Reactivation in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve is herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson sign predicts eye involvement), and reactivation in the geniculate ganglion is Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).
tileNotes: Varicella (chickenpox) is primary VZV infection, with a pruritic vesicular rash in crops at different stages.
Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of latent VZV, causing a painful vesicular rash in one dermatome.
Reactivation in the ophthalmic division of CN V can involve the eye and threaten vision; vesicles on the nose tip (Hutchinson sign) suggest ocular involvement.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, causing ear vesicles and ipsilateral facial palsy.

check.by: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
check.note: Shingles and Ramsay Hunt syndrome are standard synonyms and remove the repeated stem.

history.detail: Varicella zoster virus (VZV) causes primary varicella (chickenpox), then establishes latency in sensory ganglia. It can later reactivate as herpes zoster (shingles), which includes dermatomal forms with specific complications such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus and herpes zoster oticus. Recognizing these forms matters because ophthalmic and otic involvement can threaten vision, hearing and facial nerve function.
tileNotes: Varicella (chickenpox) is the primary VZV infection, with fever and an itchy rash of vesicles in crops at different stages. Afterward the virus stays latent in sensory ganglia.

Herpes zoster (shingles) is reactivation of latent VZV, causing a painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution, usually unilateral. Postherpetic neuralgia is a common complication, especially in older adults.

Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is zoster in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. It can involve the eye (for example keratitis or uveitis); vesicles on the nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) suggest higher risk of ocular involvement.
Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) is VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion. It classically causes ear pain, vesicles in the ear canal or auricle, and ipsilateral facial nerve palsy.

MSK-028.detail: Gluteus maximus and the three hamstrings that cross the hip (long head of biceps femoris, semimembranosus and semitendinosus) all extend the hip. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur, does not cross the hip, and acts only at the knee. Hip extension matters clinically for rising from a chair, climbing stairs and running.
tileNotes: Gluteus maximus is the large superficial buttock muscle, supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve. It is the most powerful hip extensor, especially when rising from sitting or climbing stairs.
The long head of biceps femoris arises from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. Because it crosses both joints, it extends the hip and flexes the knee.
Semimembranosus is a medial hamstring arising from the ischial tuberosity and supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

Semitendinosus is a medial hamstring with a long tendon that inserts on the medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Like the other hamstrings that cross the hip, it extends the hip and flexes the knee.

NEPH-028.detail: When bicarbonate is lost from the gut or kidney, or the kidney cannot excrete acid, chloride rises to replace it and the anion gap stays normal. Diarrhea and pancreatic fistulas lose bicarbonate-rich fluid, acetazolamide blocks proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, and distal RTA impairs distal hydrogen ion secretion. This contrasts with high-anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols, salicylates), in which an unmeasured anion accumulates.
tileNotes: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid and is the most common cause of normal-anion-gap acidosis.
Acetazolamide inhibits proximal tubule carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate wasting and normal-anion-gap acidosis.
In distal (type 1) RTA, the collecting duct cannot secrete hydrogen ions, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidemia.
Pancreatic secretions are rich in bicarbonate, so external pancreatic fistula drainage causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

check.by: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
check.note: Pancreatic fistula is a standard NAGMA cause and removes the paired RTA tiles.

history.detail: Diarrhea, acetazolamide, distal renal tubular acidosis and proximal renal tubular acidosis can each produce a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. Bicarbonate is lost from the gut or kidney, or renal acid excretion is impaired, and chloride rises to replace it, so the anion gap stays normal. This separates them from causes of high-anion-gap acidosis such as ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis.
tileNotes: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid. It is one of the most common causes of normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Its effect resembles proximal renal tubular acidosis, producing a hyperchloremic acidosis.

Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1) is impaired hydrogen ion secretion by the distal nephron. Urine pH stays inappropriately high (above about 5.5), and hypokalemia and calcium phosphate kidney stones are classic associations.

Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2) is impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. It can occur alone or as part of Fanconi syndrome, and urine can still be acidified once serum bicarbonate falls low enough.

NEU-003.detail: Damage to anterior horn cells, roots, or peripheral nerves denervates muscle. Clinically this causes atrophy, fasciculations, weakness, hyporeflexia, and reduced tone. On needle EMG, denervated muscle fibers fire spontaneously as fibrillation potentials (and positive sharp waves) a few weeks after injury. Upper motor neuron lesions instead cause spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign with little atrophy.
tileNotes: Fasciculations are visible spontaneous twitches of motor units, typical of anterior horn cell or motor axon disease.
Loss of neural trophic input and disuse causes marked muscle atrophy in lower motor neuron lesions.
Interruption of the reflex arc at the motor neuron, root, or nerve reduces or abolishes deep tendon reflexes.
Spontaneous discharges of single denervated muscle fibers appear on needle EMG a few weeks after lower motor neuron injury.

check.by: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
check.note: Fibrillation potentials are a standard LMN denervation finding; content accurate.

history.detail: Fasciculations, muscle atrophy, hyporeflexia and hypotonia are classic signs of lower motor neuron dysfunction, localizing to the anterior horn cell, nerve root or peripheral nerve. They contrast with upper motor neuron signs such as spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response. Not every peripheral neuromuscular disorder produces all four.
tileNotes: Fasciculations are brief, spontaneous, visible twitches of a group of muscle fibers supplied by one motor unit. They suggest an irritable or degenerating lower motor neuron, classically in anterior horn cell disease.
Muscle atrophy is wasting of muscle bulk. Marked atrophy follows loss of lower motor neuron innervation (denervation), unlike the milder disuse atrophy of upper motor neuron lesions.
Hyporeflexia means reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. Damage to the lower motor neuron interrupts the efferent limb of the stretch reflex arc.
Hypotonia is reduced resistance to passive movement, giving a floppy or flaccid limb. It reflects loss of the lower motor neuron drive that normally maintains resting muscle tone.

MICRO-025.detail: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a key opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, classically when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/uL. It typically causes subacute, progressive exertional dyspnea with bilateral ground-glass opacities on imaging. TMP-SMX is the classic agent for prophylaxis in appropriate patients, although the CD4 threshold is a teaching rule rather than the full prophylaxis algorithm.
tileNotes: CD4 count below 200 cells/uL indicates advanced immunosuppression in HIV infection. It is the classic teaching threshold at which Pneumocystis pneumonia risk rises and prophylaxis is considered.
Progressive exertional dyspnea is shortness of breath with activity that worsens over days to weeks. In Pneumocystis pneumonia it often comes with dry cough, fever and exertional hypoxemia.

Bilateral ground-glass lung opacities are hazy areas of increased lung density through which vessels remain visible. They are the classic imaging pattern of Pneumocystis pneumonia, though early chest radiographs can be normal.
TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is the preferred agent for both prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia. Prophylaxis also helps protect against toxoplasmosis.

PLX-BCH-007.detail: Types I, II, III and V are fibril-forming collagens: their triple helices assemble into cross-linked fibrils that give tissues tensile strength. This sets them apart from network-forming type IV collagen of basement membranes and anchoring type VII collagen. Mutations in fibrillar collagens underlie classic exam diseases such as osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.
tileNotes: Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen, found in bone, skin, tendon and late wound repair. Defects in type I collagen synthesis cause osteogenesis imperfecta.
Type II collagen is the main collagen of cartilage, and is also present in the vitreous body and nucleus pulposus. It forms thin fibrils that give these tissues tensile strength.

Edema of the intestinal wall causes episodes of severe, crampy abdominal pain, sometimes with vomiting. These attacks can mimic a surgical abdomen and are a classic presentation of this disorder.

PLEXUS-GEN-009.detail: These four enzymes carry out short-patch base excision repair (BER) in sequence: a damaged base is removed, the abasic site is cut, the one-nucleotide gap is filled, and the nick is sealed. BER corrects small lesions that do not distort the helix, such as uracil from cytosine deamination and oxidized or alkylated bases, which sets it apart from repair of bulky lesions like thymine dimers.
tileNotes: A DNA glycosylase recognizes a specific damaged or inappropriate base (for example uracil in DNA) and cleaves its bond to the sugar. This first step leaves an apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP), or abasic, site.
AP endonuclease recognizes the abasic site left by the glycosylase and cuts the sugar-phosphate backbone there. The resulting nick gives the polymerase a place to start repair.
DNA polymerase beta is a repair polymerase that inserts the single missing nucleotide in short-patch BER. It also removes the leftover deoxyribose-phosphate remnant before the strand is sealed.
DNA ligase forms the final phosphodiester bond that seals the nick, restoring an intact strand. Ligases also act in DNA replication and in other repair pathways, so this step is not unique to BER.

Its deficiency therefore causes megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and raises homocysteine, while methylmalonic acid stays normal because methylmalonyl-CoA mutase depends on vitamin B12, not folate. Hypersegmented neutrophils have an unusually high number of nuclear lobes, often five or more. They are a classic peripheral smear sign of a megaloblastic process and appear in both folate and B12 deficiency.

MICRO-038.detail: Ivermectin acts on glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle, paralyzing susceptible worms and arthropods, and it has treatment roles in all four of these infections. Its role is not identical across them: route, first-line status, and alternatives differ by indication and patient. Before treating onchocerciasis, clinicians screen for Loa loa co-infection, because treating heavy Loa loa microfilaremia can cause severe reactions.
tileNotes: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) is caused by the filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus, spread by blackfly bites, and causes itchy dermatitis, skin nodules, and eye damage. Ivermectin kills the microfilariae, after screening for Loa loa co-infection.

Strongyloidiasis is infection with Strongyloides stercoralis, whose larvae penetrate the skin and can persist for years through autoinfection. Ivermectin is the treatment of choice, which matters because corticosteroids or immunosuppression can trigger life-threatening hyperinfection.

Scabies is an intensely itchy skin infestation by the burrowing mite Sarcoptes scabiei, classically affecting finger webs and worse at night. Oral ivermectin is an option alongside topical agents such as permethrin, and is often used for crusted scabies or outbreaks.

Pediculosis capitis is head lice infestation, causing scalp itching with nits attached to hair shafts. Topical ivermectin lotion is an approved treatment, while oral ivermectin is an off-label option, and the two are not interchangeable first-line choices.

ENDO-012.detail: Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, driving excess thyroid hormone production and a diffusely enlarged, overactive gland. Receptor-related autoimmunity also affects orbital and pretibial connective tissue, causing eye and skin changes that are specific to Graves among causes of hyperthyroidism, although not every patient develops them. Diffusely increased radioiodine uptake helps distinguish Graves from nodular disease and thyroiditis.
tileNotes: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) bind and activate the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH. They cause the hyperthyroidism of Graves disease and are a classic example of type II hypersensitivity with stimulatory antibodies.

Exophthalmos is forward protrusion of the eyes, here caused by inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition in orbital tissue and extraocular muscles. It is a feature of Graves orbitopathy, which not all patients have.

Pretibial myxedema is a non-pitting, thickened, sometimes orange-peel textured skin change over the shins from glycosaminoglycan deposition. It is a characteristic but relatively uncommon Graves dermopathy.

Diffuse increased radioiodine uptake means the whole gland takes up more iodine than normal on a thyroid scan, reflecting uniform antibody-driven stimulation. This contrasts with patchy uptake in toxic multinodular goiter and low uptake in thyroiditis.

NEU-039.detail: Bridging veins cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses, and acceleration-deceleration forces can tear them. Because the collection lies beneath the dura, it is not limited by sutures and spreads over the hemisphere as a crescent on CT, though it does not cross the midline falx. Brain atrophy in older adults and people with chronic alcohol use stretches the veins and widens the subdural space, increasing risk; infants (abusive head trauma) and anticoagulated patients are also at risk. Epidural hematoma is the contrast: arterial, above the dura, and bounded by sutures.

The blood collects in the subdural space between the inner dural layer and the arachnoid.

Cerebral atrophy stretches the bridging veins across a wider subdural space, so older adults can develop a subdural hematoma after minor trauma, often chronic.

GI-023.detail: Wilson disease results from ATP7B mutations that impair biliary copper excretion, so copper accumulates in the liver, brain, and cornea. Each of these therapies lowers body copper burden, but by different mechanisms: chelators increase urinary excretion, zinc blocks intestinal absorption, and diet limits intake. They have different roles and are not interchangeable, nor are they all used together, and treatment is lifelong.
tileNotes: Penicillamine is a copper chelator that binds copper and increases its excretion in urine. It is effective but has frequent adverse effects, including hypersensitivity reactions, proteinuria, and bone marrow suppression.
Trientine is another copper chelator that promotes urinary copper excretion. It is commonly used as an alternative to penicillamine, particularly when penicillamine is not tolerated.

Zinc salts induce metallothionein in intestinal cells; this protein binds dietary copper, which is then lost in stool as the cells are shed. Zinc reduces copper absorption rather than removing stored copper and is often used for maintenance.
A low-copper diet means limiting copper-rich foods such as shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate, and mushrooms. It is an adjunct that reduces intake and is not sufficient as the sole treatment.

IMM-014.detail: IgE binds with high affinity to Fc epsilon receptor I on mast cells and basophils, sensitizing these cells. When a multivalent allergen later crosslinks the bound IgE, the cells degranulate within minutes, producing type I (immediate) hypersensitivity such as allergic rhinitis, asthma, or anaphylaxis. The same IgE-based system also contributes to host defense against helminths, together with eosinophils.
tileNotes: Mast-cell Fc receptor binding refers to the Fc portion of IgE attaching to the high-affinity receptor Fc epsilon RI on mast cells and basophils. This arms the cells in advance, so IgE sits on them even without antigen present.

Allergen-induced crosslinking occurs when an allergen bridges two or more receptor-bound IgE molecules. This triggers signaling that releases preformed mediators such as histamine and starts synthesis of leukotrienes and prostaglandins.

Type I hypersensitivity is the immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction that requires prior sensitization and begins within minutes of re-exposure. A late-phase reaction can follow hours later as recruited inflammatory cells arrive.

Injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier lets protein-rich fluid flood the alveoli, forming hyaline membranes, while surfactant dysfunction promotes alveolar collapse and stiff, poorly compliant lungs. IMM-001.detail: The spleen, lymph nodes, Peyer's patches and tonsils are secondary (peripheral) lymphoid tissues. Lymphocytes develop in the primary lymphoid organs, the bone marrow and thymus, and then circulate to secondary tissues, where mature lymphocytes meet antigen and mount adaptive immune responses. Each secondary tissue samples antigen from a different compartment, such as blood, lymph or mucosal surfaces.

Ulcers and tumors cause iron deficiency only when they bleed. ENDO-009.detail: Acromegaly is caused by excess growth hormone, usually from a pituitary adenoma, after the growth plates have closed. Treatment aims to remove the tumor or control GH and IGF-1: transsphenoidal resection is first-line, while somatostatin analogues, dopamine agonists and GH receptor antagonists are medical options when surgery is not curative or not possible.

Cabergoline is a dopamine (D2) agonist that can modestly suppress GH secretion. It is less potent than somatostatin analogues and is used as an adjunctive option, especially in milder disease.

CARD-001.detail: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, which produces all four defects together. The severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction largely determines how much deoxygenated blood shunts right to left across the VSD, and therefore how cyanotic the child is. It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion, and squatting relieves hypercyanotic spells by raising systemic vascular resistance.
tileNotes: Narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract (often infundibular, sometimes valvular) limits blood flow to the lungs. Its severity is the main determinant of right-to-left shunting and cyanosis in tetralogy of Fallot.
An overriding aorta sits above the ventricular septal defect, so it receives blood from both ventricles. This lets deoxygenated right ventricular blood enter the systemic circulation.
A ventricular septal defect is an opening in the wall between the ventricles. In tetralogy it is typically large, allowing pressures to equalize and blood to shunt according to outflow resistance.
Thickening of the right ventricular wall develops because the right ventricle pumps against outflow obstruction. On chest radiograph it contributes to the classic boot-shaped heart.

CARD-002.detail: High-output heart failure occurs when the heart, though often normal, cannot keep up with a markedly increased demand for cardiac output, typically because systemic vascular resistance is low or metabolic needs are high. Thiamine deficiency, severe anemia, hyperthyroidism and a hemodynamically significant arteriovenous fistula are classic examples. None invariably causes heart failure; the state must be severe or prolonged enough to overwhelm cardiac reserve.
tileNotes: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency can cause wet beriberi, in which peripheral vasodilation lowers vascular resistance and drives a high-output state. It is classically seen with chronic alcohol use or malnutrition.
When anemia is severe, reduced oxygen-carrying capacity triggers vasodilation and a compensatory rise in cardiac output. Over time this increased workload can lead to high-output failure.
Excess thyroid hormone raises metabolic demand, heart rate and contractility while lowering vascular resistance. This hyperdynamic circulation can progress to high-output heart failure.

An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses capillaries. A large, hemodynamically significant fistula creates a low-resistance circuit that forces cardiac output to rise.

CARD-003.detail: Nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine and amlodipine are dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, recognizable by the -dipine suffix. They block L-type calcium channels mainly in vascular smooth muscle, causing arteriolar dilation with relatively little direct effect on cardiac conduction. This contrasts with the nondihydropyridines verapamil and diltiazem, and explains typical side effects such as peripheral edema, flushing, headache and reflex tachycardia.

Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine widely used for hypertension and stable angina. Dose-related ankle edema from arteriolar dilation is a common, well-known side effect.

CARD-032.detail: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, often viral or idiopathic. It classically causes sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, a scratchy friction rub, diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG. CARD-033.detail: In constrictive pericarditis, a thickened, often fibrotic pericardium encases the heart and limits filling in mid to late diastole. Early filling is rapid and then stops abruptly, causing a pericardial knock and a steep y descent. Inspiration fails to lower jugular pressure (Kussmaul sign). Kussmaul sign and rapid y descent also occur in restrictive cardiomyopathy, whereas pericardial calcification and a knock favor constriction.

Kussmaul sign is a rise, or failure to fall, of jugular venous pressure with inspiration. A rigid pericardium prevents the right heart from accepting increased venous return.
A calcified pericardium may appear as a rim of calcium around the heart on radiograph or CT. When present it strongly supports constriction, though many cases lack calcification.
A rapid jugular y descent reflects brisk early diastolic emptying of the right atrium before filling is abruptly limited. It contrasts with the blunted y descent of tamponade.

CARD-041.detail: In atherosclerosis, vascular smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima, proliferate and lay down extracellular matrix, forming the fibrous cap of the plaque. PDGF and FGF act directly as mitogens and chemoattractants, while endothelin-1 and interleukin-1 contribute more indirectly by enhancing migration or promoting phenotypic switching. Understanding these signals explains how a fatty streak evolves into a fibrous plaque.

Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor peptide produced by endothelial cells. In plaque development it acts more indirectly, potentiating PDGF-driven smooth muscle cell migration.

Interleukin-1 is a proinflammatory cytokine released by activated macrophages. It promotes smooth muscle cell phenotypic switching and upregulates PDGF receptors, an indirect contribution to recruitment.

CARD-044.detail: Several endocrine disorders raise blood pressure through hormone excess: cortisol in Cushing syndrome, aldosterone in hyperaldosteronism, catecholamines in pheochromocytoma and thyroid hormone in hyperthyroidism. Recognizing these is important because treating the underlying disorder can improve or cure the hypertension. Clues include young onset, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia or episodic symptoms.

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor, usually of the adrenal medulla. It classically causes episodic or sustained hypertension with headache, sweating and palpitations.
Hyperthyroidism increases heart rate, contractility and cardiac output. The resulting hypertension is often predominantly systolic with a wide pulse pressure.

CARD-045.detail: Hypovolemic shock results from a substantial loss of effective circulating volume, reducing preload, stroke volume and tissue perfusion. Bleeding from trauma or the upper gastrointestinal tract causes hemorrhagic losses, severe diarrhea causes fluid and electrolyte losses, and major burns combine fluid loss with large shifts into tissues. Recognizing the cause guides replacement with blood products or crystalloid and control of ongoing losses.
tileNotes: Traumatic hemorrhage is major blood loss after injury, external or internal. It is the classic cause of hemorrhagic, and therefore hypovolemic, shock.
Upper gastrointestinal bleeding arises proximal to the ligament of Treitz, for example from peptic ulcers or varices. Brisk bleeding can rapidly deplete circulating volume.
Severe diarrhea, as in cholera, can cause large losses of water and electrolytes. Without adequate replacement, volume depletion can progress to shock.
A major burn injury damages skin and capillaries, causing fluid leak into tissues and evaporative losses. Large burns require aggressive fluid resuscitation to prevent shock.

CARD-046.detail: The specialized conduction system starts each heartbeat and coordinates contraction. The sinoatrial node generates the impulse, the atrioventricular node delays it so the ventricles can fill, and the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje network distribute it rapidly through the ventricles. Disease at each level produces characteristic arrhythmias, such as sinus node dysfunction or AV block.
tileNotes: The sinoatrial node, located in the right atrium near the superior vena cava, is the normal pacemaker. Its cells depolarize spontaneously, setting the heart rate.
The atrioventricular node lies near the interatrial septum and conducts slowly. This delay, seen as part of the PR interval, allows ventricular filling before contraction.
The bundle of His carries the impulse from the AV node through the fibrous skeleton into the ventricular septum. It then divides into the right and left bundle branches.
The Purkinje network consists of fast-conducting fibers spreading through the ventricular subendocardium. Rapid conduction allows nearly simultaneous ventricular contraction.

CARD-047.detail: A ventricular pressure-volume loop plots pressure against volume through one cardiac cycle. With normal valves it has four phases: isovolumetric contraction after mitral closure, ejection after aortic opening, isovolumetric relaxation after aortic closure, and filling after mitral opening. Changes in loop shape are used to illustrate effects of altered preload, afterload, contractility and valve disease.
tileNotes: Isovolumetric contraction begins when the mitral valve closes. The ventricle contracts with both valves shut, so pressure rises steeply while volume stays constant.
Ventricular ejection starts when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens. Volume falls as blood is pumped out, and stroke volume is the loop width.
Isovolumetric relaxation begins with aortic valve closure. Pressure falls rapidly with both valves closed and volume unchanged at end-systolic volume.

DERM-001.detail: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells all reside in the epidermis but perform distinct functions: structural barrier, pigment production, antigen presentation and touch sensation. They also have different embryologic origins, so they are linked by location rather than lineage. Each population is linked to characteristic diseases, such as melanoma arising from melanocytes.

Itraconazole is an oral azole antifungal that inhibits ergosterol synthesis. It is the usual first-line treatment for cutaneous and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

Nail involvement is a recognized clue to joint disease risk, linking dermatology and rheumatology.
tileNotes: Psoriatic plaques are sharply defined, raised red patches covered with silvery-white scale. They classically occur on the elbows, knees, scalp and lower back.
The Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding when the scale is scraped off a psoriatic plaque. It reflects dilated capillaries close to the surface beneath a thinned epidermis.
Nail pitting is small depressions in the nail surface from abnormal nail matrix growth. It is common in psoriasis, and other nail changes include oil-drop spots and onycholysis.

Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis seen in a subset of people with psoriasis, typically seronegative for rheumatoid factor. It can cause dactylitis (sausage digits) and distal interphalangeal joint disease.

DERM-030.detail: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arises from keratinocytes and is most often driven by cumulative UV exposure, but several other settings raise risk. Long-standing wounds and scars can undergo malignant change (Marjolin ulcer), arsenic is a known carcinogen, and immunosuppression, especially after organ transplantation, markedly increases incidence. A nonhealing or changing lesion in these settings warrants biopsy.
tileNotes: Chronic wounds, such as long-standing ulcers or draining sinuses, involve persistent injury and repair. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma can occur after many years.
Burn scars can develop aggressive carcinoma decades after the injury, a lesion called a Marjolin ulcer. Squamous cell carcinoma is the usual tumor type, so a new ulcer in an old scar needs biopsy.
Arsenic is a carcinogen encountered through contaminated well water or certain occupations. It is linked to cutaneous SCC and to arsenical keratoses of the palms and soles.
Immunosuppression, particularly in organ transplant recipients, markedly raises the risk of cutaneous SCC. Reduced immune surveillance allows UV-damaged and HPV-infected cells to progress.

DERM-031.detail: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and arises from basal keratinocytes in sun-exposed skin, especially the face. It classically appears as a pearly papule with fine surface vessels, sometimes with a central ulcer (rodent ulcer). It grows slowly and very rarely metastasizes, but untreated tumors can locally destroy surrounding tissue.
tileNotes: A pearly lesion has a translucent, shiny surface like a pearl. This appearance is the classic clinical clue for nodular basal cell carcinoma, often with a rolled border.
Telangiectasias are small, dilated superficial blood vessels. Fine branching vessels across the surface of a pearly papule strongly suggest basal cell carcinoma.

Peripheral palisading means the outermost tumor cells of each nest line up in a neat row, like a picket fence. It is the classic histologic feature of basal cell carcinoma, often with retraction clefts.
Basal cell carcinoma usually enlarges slowly over months to years and very rarely spreads to distant sites. Slow growth does not mean harmless, since neglected tumors can invade local structures.

DERM-032.detail: Keratoacanthoma is a keratinocyte tumor that grows rapidly over weeks into a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, most often on sun-exposed skin of older adults. Some regress on their own, but it overlaps clinically and histologically with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. For that reason, excision or biopsy rather than observation is the standard approach.
tileNotes: Keratoacanthoma forms a firm, symmetric, dome-shaped nodule, usually on sun-exposed skin. Its smooth shape with a central crater is the classic clinical appearance.
The center of the lesion contains a plug of keratin, giving a crater-like or volcano appearance. This feature is shared with crateriform squamous cell carcinoma.
Rapid enlargement over a few weeks is the hallmark of keratoacanthoma. Such fast growth distinguishes it from the slow course of basal cell carcinoma.
Some keratoacanthomas involute spontaneously over months, often leaving a scar. Regression is possible but not reliable, and the lesion should still be excised or biopsied to exclude SCC.

DERM-033.detail: Melanoma arises from melanocytes, and four classic subtypes are taught based on growth pattern and location. Superficial spreading is the most common, nodular grows vertically early, lentigo maligna melanoma arises on chronically sun-damaged skin of older adults, and acral lentiginous occurs on palms, soles and nail beds. Prognosis depends mainly on Breslow depth, not subtype alone.
tileNotes: Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common subtype, with a prolonged horizontal (radial) growth phase. It often appears as an enlarging, irregular, variably pigmented patch on the trunk or legs.
Nodular melanoma enters the vertical growth phase early, forming a raised, often dark or sometimes amelanotic nodule. Early depth gives it a worse outlook at diagnosis.
Lentigo maligna melanoma is the invasive form of lentigo maligna, arising on chronically sun-damaged skin such as the face of older adults. Its in situ precursor can grow slowly for years.
Acral lentiginous melanoma arises on the palms, soles or under the nails. It occurs in all skin types and is the most common subtype in people with darker skin.

DERM-035.detail: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana, seen mainly in people with advanced HIV or other immunosuppression. It produces red to purple vascular papules that can mimic Kaposi sarcoma or pyogenic granuloma. Biopsy distinguishes them, showing neutrophils and bacteria visible on silver stain, and the infection responds to antibiotics.
tileNotes: Bartonella are gram-negative bacteria; B. henselae is linked to cat scratches and B. quintana to body lice. In immunocompromised hosts they can stimulate blood vessel proliferation.
The skin lesions are bright red to violaceous, dome-shaped vascular papules or nodules that may bleed. They resemble Kaposi sarcoma, so biopsy is needed to tell them apart.
Warthin-Starry is a silver stain that highlights the bacteria as dark clusters in tissue. It supports the diagnosis of bacillary angiomatosis, though it is not perfectly specific or always positive.
Neutrophils clustered around bacterial aggregates are a frequent histologic feature of bacillary angiomatosis. This inflammatory infiltrate helps distinguish it from Kaposi sarcoma.

DERM-036.detail: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor caused by HHV-8 (KSHV), which is present in all forms of the disease. It appears as purple patches, plaques or nodules on skin and can involve mucosa and viscera. HIV-associated immunosuppression greatly increases risk, but classic, endemic and transplant-related forms also occur, so HIV and HHV-8 play different roles.
tileNotes: HHV-8, also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, is the causative virus in every form of Kaposi sarcoma. Its proteins drive proliferation of infected endothelial-derived spindle cells.
Kaposi sarcoma lesions are purple to red-brown patches, plaques or nodules, often on the legs, face or oral mucosa. Their violaceous color reflects their vascular nature.
Histology shows proliferating spindle-shaped cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells. Immunostaining for HHV-8 in these cells confirms the diagnosis.
HIV-associated immunosuppression greatly increases the risk of Kaposi sarcoma, which is an AIDS-defining illness. It is a risk context rather than the cause, since HHV-8 is required.

DERM-037.detail: Acanthosis nigricans is thickened, velvety, darkened skin, usually in body folds such as the neck and axillae. Most cases are benign and reflect insulin resistance, as in obesity and type 2 diabetes. A sudden, extensive onset, especially in an older adult without obesity, can instead signal an internal malignancy, classically gastric adenocarcinoma.

Malignant acanthosis nigricans is rare and classically linked to gastric adenocarcinoma. Abrupt, widespread onset or mucosal involvement should prompt a search for cancer, but most cases are benign.

ENDO-001.detail: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary through hormones released into the hypophyseal portal circulation. These four are stimulatory releasing hormones, each driving a specific pituitary axis. Dopamine and somatostatin are the main inhibitory counterparts. Knowing the pairings helps localize endocrine disorders as hypothalamic, pituitary or target-gland problems.
tileNotes: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates TSH release from the anterior pituitary. It also stimulates prolactin, which helps explain hyperprolactinemia in primary hypothyroidism.
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulates LH and FSH release. It must be pulsatile, since continuous GnRH agonist exposure suppresses the axis, a principle used in treating prostate cancer.
Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulates ACTH release from pituitary corticotrophs. It is part of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that controls cortisol.
Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) stimulates GH secretion from somatotrophs. Somatostatin opposes it, and GHRH-secreting tumors are a rare cause of acromegaly.

ENDO-002.detail: These are the tropic hormones of the anterior pituitary: each acts on another endocrine gland to stimulate its hormone output. TSH drives the thyroid, ACTH the adrenal cortex, and FSH and LH the gonads. Growth hormone and prolactin act mainly on non-endocrine tissues. Tropic hormones underlie negative feedback loops that are used to localize endocrine disease.
tileNotes: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulates thyroid growth and the synthesis and release of T4 and T3. It is the main screening test for thyroid function, rising in primary hypothyroidism and falling in primary hyperthyroidism.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulates the adrenal cortex, mainly to produce cortisol. It is a peptide derived from POMC, and excess ACTH can cause hyperpigmentation.

Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts on ovarian granulosa cells to support follicle development and on testicular Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis. It is controlled by GnRH and inhibited by inhibin.

Luteinizing hormone (LH) stimulates ovarian theca cells and testicular Leydig cells to produce sex steroids, and its midcycle surge triggers ovulation. Together with FSH, it links the pituitary to gonadal endocrine function.

ENDO-003.detail: SIADH is excess ADH release despite low plasma osmolality, causing water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine. Causes include ectopic ADH from tumors, especially small cell lung carcinoma, and a range of drugs. Identifying and removing a drug cause is an early step in management, alongside fluid restriction.
tileNotes: Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly linked to smoking. It can secrete ADH ectopically, making it the classic malignant cause of SIADH.
Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapy and immunosuppressive agent. It is a recognized drug cause of SIADH, and hemorrhagic cystitis is its other classic adverse effect.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely used antidepressants. They can cause SIADH and hyponatremia, particularly in older adults.
Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant also used for trigeminal neuralgia and bipolar disorder. It can cause SIADH with hyponatremia, among other adverse effects such as agranulocytosis.

ENDO-005.detail: Central diabetes insipidus is deficient ADH secretion from damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, causing polyuria of dilute urine and thirst. Acquired causes include trauma, vascular events, infection, infiltrative disease, tumors and surgery. On water deprivation testing, urine fails to concentrate but does concentrate after desmopressin, distinguishing it from nephrogenic DI.
tileNotes: Traumatic brain injury can damage the pituitary stalk, hypothalamus or posterior pituitary. Central DI can follow, sometimes transiently, after head injury.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage is bleeding into the space around the brain, most often from a ruptured aneurysm. It can disrupt hypothalamic function and cause central DI, though hyponatremia is also common after SAH.
Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, usually from infection. Involvement of the basal brain or hypothalamic region can impair ADH production and cause central DI.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can infiltrate bone and other organs. Involvement of the pituitary stalk or hypothalamus is a classic cause of central DI, especially in children.

ENDO-006.detail: Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin release from lactotrophs via D2 receptors. Drugs that block D2 receptors remove this inhibition, raising prolactin and potentially causing galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, reduced libido and infertility. Antipsychotics and antiemetic prokinetics are classic culprits, so a medication history is essential before imaging for hyperprolactinemia.
tileNotes: Risperidone is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic. Among atypical agents it is notable for raising prolactin, due to D2 blockade including at the pituitary.
Haloperidol is a high-potency first-generation antipsychotic and a strong D2 antagonist. Its D2 blockade can cause hyperprolactinemia and extrapyramidal side effects.
Fluphenazine is a high-potency typical antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class. Like other strong D2 blockers, it can elevate prolactin.

Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist used as an antiemetic and prokinetic for gastroparesis. It can elevate prolactin and cause extrapyramidal effects, showing that this effect is not limited to antipsychotics.

ENDO-007.detail: Hypopituitarism is deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones. Structural causes include ischemia, hemorrhage, compression by tumors and loss of pituitary tissue. Deficiencies can appear gradually or acutely, and secondary adrenal insufficiency is the most dangerous because it can be life-threatening. Empty sella is often an incidental finding with normal function.
tileNotes: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of the pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage, since the gland enlarges in pregnancy. Failure to lactate is a classic early clue.

Empty sella syndrome is a sella turcica that appears filled with CSF, with a flattened pituitary. It is often incidental with normal function, but it can be associated with pituitary hormone deficiency.

Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary, usually within an existing adenoma. It presents with sudden headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia, and acute adrenal insufficiency is the key danger.

Craniopharyngioma is a benign suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch remnants, with peaks in childhood and later adulthood. It can compress the pituitary and optic chiasm, and calcification on imaging is a classic clue.

ENDO-008.detail: Acromegaly results from excess growth hormone after the epiphyseal growth plates have closed, usually from a pituitary adenoma. Because long bones can no longer lengthen, GH and IGF-1 enlarge bone and soft tissue, coarsening the face and enlarging the hands and feet. The same excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism. Changes develop slowly, so diagnosis is often delayed.
tileNotes: Frontal bossing is prominence of the forehead from bony overgrowth of the frontal bone. It contributes to the coarse facial appearance of acromegaly.
Mandibular enlargement causes a protruding jaw (prognathism) and changes in the bite. It is a classic facial feature of GH excess in adults.
Widened spaces between the teeth develop as the jaw enlarges while the teeth stay the same size. Patients may notice new gaps or a changed bite.
Acral enlargement means growth of the hands and feet, often noticed as increasing ring, glove or shoe size. It reflects soft-tissue and bone growth from GH and IGF-1 excess.

ENDO-015.detail: Congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid hormone deficiency present at birth, most often from thyroid dysgenesis. Infants may look normal at first, but untreated deficiency produces these features along with poor feeding, prolonged jaundice and constipation. ENDO-016.detail: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer and is diagnosed mainly by its characteristic nuclear features rather than by architecture alone. It often spreads to cervical lymph nodes and generally has an excellent prognosis. BRAF mutations and RET/PTC rearrangements are alternative, typically mutually exclusive drivers, and somatic RET/PTC differs from the germline RET mutations of MEN2.

ENDO-017.detail: Follicular thyroid carcinoma cannot be distinguished from follicular adenoma by cytology alone, because both are made of follicles. The diagnosis requires capsular or vascular invasion on histology of the excised nodule, which is why fine-needle aspiration is often indeterminate. Unlike papillary carcinoma, it tends to spread through the blood to bone and lung rather than to lymph nodes.

Hematogenous dissemination is spread through the bloodstream. Follicular carcinoma commonly metastasizes this way to bone and lung, whereas papillary carcinoma favors lymphatic spread.

ENDO-018.detail: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of the calcitonin-producing parafollicular C cells, not of follicular cells. Calcitonin serves as a tumor marker, and the tumor can contain amyloid derived from calcitonin. ENDO-019.detail: Calcium stabilizes nerve membranes by raising the threshold for depolarization, so low ionized calcium makes nerves and muscles hyperexcitable. This produces perioral and fingertip tingling, muscle cramps, tetany and the Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and in severe cases seizures, laryngospasm or arrhythmias. Hypoparathyroidism, such as after thyroid surgery, is one important cause among several.
tileNotes: The Chvostek sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear. It suggests neuromuscular irritability but is nonspecific, appearing in some people with normal calcium.
The Trousseau sign is carpal spasm induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for a few minutes. It is more specific than the Chvostek sign for hypocalcemia.
Tetany is involuntary sustained muscle contraction, such as carpopedal spasm. It is the classic manifestation of hypocalcemic neuromuscular excitability.
Seizures can occur when hypocalcemia is severe or develops rapidly, reflecting increased neuronal excitability. Correcting the calcium is key, since anticonvulsants alone may not control them.

ENDO-022.detail: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and absorbed in the small intestine with dietary fat, so conditions that impair fat absorption predispose to deficiency. These include mucosal disease, pancreatic insufficiency and surgical bypass of absorptive bowel. The consequences are reduced calcium absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism and bone disease such as osteomalacia, so at-risk patients are often screened and supplemented.
tileNotes: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages small intestinal villi, especially in the proximal bowel. The resulting malabsorption can cause vitamin D and calcium deficiency and reduced bone density.
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic CFTR disorder that commonly causes pancreatic insufficiency. Without pancreatic enzymes, fat and fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin D, are poorly absorbed.

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease involving the small bowel or prior resection raises the risk of vitamin D deficiency, although not every patient is affected.

Gastric bypass is bariatric surgery that reroutes food past most of the stomach, the duodenum and part of the jejunum. Reduced absorptive surface predisposes to vitamin D and calcium deficiency, so long-term supplementation is standard.

ENDO-031.detail: These four enzyme deficiencies all follow autosomal recessive inheritance and all disrupt sex-steroid synthesis or androgen activation, so they appear in the workup of differences in sex development. The first three are forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia affecting adrenal steroidogenesis. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is not congenital adrenal hyperplasia; it impairs peripheral conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone.

ENDO-035.detail: In 46,XY individuals with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, testosterone is made normally but poorly converted to dihydrotestosterone. Testosterone-dependent internal male structures develop, while DHT-dependent external genitalia may be undervirilized at birth. The rise in testosterone at puberty can then cause substantial virilization, and an elevated testosterone-to-DHT ratio supports the diagnosis.

Virilization at puberty refers to masculinizing changes such as voice deepening and increased muscle mass. Rising pubertal testosterone can produce these changes even though DHT remains low.

ENDO-036.detail: Insulin is the body's main anabolic hormone, signaling after meals to store fuel. It promotes glycogen, lipid and protein synthesis and, in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, moves GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface to increase glucose uptake. Knowing these actions explains the catabolic picture of insulin deficiency, such as hyperglycemia, lipolysis and muscle wasting.
tileNotes: Glycogen synthesis is the storage of glucose as glycogen, mainly in liver and muscle. Insulin activates glycogen synthase, promoting this storage after meals.
Lipid synthesis (lipogenesis) is the formation of fatty acids and triglycerides. Insulin stimulates it and simultaneously inhibits lipolysis, favoring fat storage in adipose tissue.

Protein synthesis is the building of proteins from amino acids. Insulin increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis while reducing protein breakdown, an anabolic effect seen especially in muscle.

GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive glucose transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Insulin signaling moves GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake in these tissues.

ENDO-037.detail: These organ-specific autoimmune diseases tend to occur together in the same patients and families, partly through shared HLA class II risk haplotypes such as DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8. Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes defines autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2, and celiac disease is a frequently associated condition rather than a defining criterion. Hashimoto thyroiditis is autoimmune destruction of the thyroid, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. Autoimmune thyroid disease is a frequent component of APS-2.

Glomerular basement membrane thickening is an early change, followed by mesangial expansion and glomerulosclerosis, which may be nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules). ENDO-039.detail: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state share many triggers, usually physiologic stress that raises counterregulatory hormones or inadequate insulin action. ENDO-040.detail: Diabetic ketoacidosis results from insulin deficiency with excess counterregulatory hormones, which drives lipolysis and hepatic ketone production. Accumulating ketoacids produce an anion gap metabolic acidosis, the lungs compensate with deep, rapid breathing, and exhaled acetone gives a fruity odor. Other ketoacidoses, such as alcoholic or starvation ketoacidosis, can share some features, so the diabetes context matters; not every finding appears in every case.

Ketonemia means ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) in the blood. In DKA, insulin deficiency allows unchecked fatty acid oxidation and ketone production by the liver.
An anion gap metabolic acidosis is a fall in blood pH and bicarbonate with an increase in unmeasured anions. In DKA the unmeasured anions are ketoacids.

GI-006.detail: Macroglossia, an abnormally large tongue, can result from tissue overgrowth, infiltration or deposition. Acromegaly enlarges soft tissues through excess growth hormone and IGF-1, hypothyroidism causes myxedematous infiltration, amyloidosis deposits abnormal protein, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome causes congenital overgrowth. Macroglossia is an association rather than a universal finding in each, but in an adult it should prompt consideration of amyloidosis in particular.
tileNotes: Acromegaly is excess growth hormone after growth plate closure, usually from a pituitary adenoma. It enlarges soft tissues, hands, feet and jaw, and the tongue can become enlarged.
Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone. Accumulation of glycosaminoglycan-rich myxedematous tissue can enlarge the tongue, a feature also seen in congenital hypothyroidism.
Amyloidosis is extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils. In AL amyloidosis especially, tongue infiltration is a classic cause of acquired macroglossia in adults.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a congenital overgrowth disorder involving imprinting abnormalities on chromosome 11p15. Macroglossia is one of its most common features, along with abdominal wall defects and an increased risk of Wilms tumor.

GI-008.detail: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder caused by loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide and VIP. Without them, the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost, producing dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Barium study classically shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird-beak, but diagnosis is confirmed by manometry, and pseudoachalasia from malignancy must be excluded.

Impaired LES relaxation means the lower esophageal sphincter does not open fully on swallowing. On manometry it appears as an elevated integrated relaxation pressure, a key diagnostic finding.
Bird-beak narrowing is the smooth, tapered distal esophagus seen on barium swallow above a dilated proximal esophagus. It is a classic but not pathognomonic achalasia image.

Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the onset suggests a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction. In achalasia, both pass poorly because of absent peristalsis and a nonrelaxing sphincter.

history.detail: Vitamin B12 absorption depends on several GI steps, and a defect at any stage can cause deficiency. GI-015.detail: Menetrier disease is a rare hyperplastic gastropathy driven by excess TGF-alpha signaling through the EGF receptor. Mucus-secreting foveolar cells proliferate, producing giant rugal folds, while parietal cells are reduced. The thickened mucosa leaks protein, causing protein-losing gastropathy with hypoalbuminemia and edema; histology helps distinguish it from other causes of enlarged folds such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome or lymphoma.

Protein-losing gastropathy is excessive loss of plasma proteins through the gastric mucosa. In Menetrier disease the hyperplastic mucosa leaks protein into the stomach lumen.
Hypoalbuminemia is a low serum albumin. It results from gastric protein loss in Menetrier disease and can cause peripheral edema.

GI-017.detail: Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase of gastric parietal cells, the final step of acid secretion. They are prodrugs activated in the acidic canaliculus and bind covalently to active pumps, so acid secretion recovers only as new pumps are made. This makes them the most potent acid suppressants, used for GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori regimens and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that, like the others, covalently binds activated proton pumps to suppress acid secretion.
Esomeprazole is the S-enantiomer of omeprazole. It shares the same irreversible proton pump inhibition mechanism.

GI-019.detail: Cimetidine, an H2 receptor antagonist, has several classic side effects that set it apart from other drugs in its class. It is therefore most vulnerable to ischemia and to drugs that form toxic metabolites, such as acetaminophen and halothane. Alcohol-related injury also tends to be centrilobular, though severe injury of any cause can extend beyond zone 3.

GI-022.detail: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7B mutations. Defective copper excretion into bile and impaired incorporation into ceruloplasmin lead to copper accumulation in the liver, brain and cornea, with low serum ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper. Increased urinary copper, measured over 24 hours, reflects excess free circulating copper being filtered by the kidney. It is a useful supportive test in Wilson disease.

Kayser-Fleischer rings are golden-brown copper deposits in Descemet membrane at the corneal edge, often seen by slit-lamp exam. They are common with neurologic involvement but frequently absent in hepatic presentations.

GI-024.detail: Hereditary hemochromatosis causes excess intestinal iron absorption, usually from HFE mutations that lower hepcidin. Serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation rise, while TIBC, a measure of available transferrin binding sites, is typically reduced. Transferrin saturation is the usual screening test; ferritin reflects iron stores but is also an acute-phase reactant, and the same pattern can occur in secondary iron overload.
tileNotes: Serum iron is the amount of iron circulating bound to transferrin. It is elevated in hemochromatosis because absorption exceeds the body's needs.

Ferritin is the main intracellular iron storage protein, and its serum level roughly reflects total body iron stores. It is high in hemochromatosis but can also rise with inflammation, liver disease or malignancy.
Transferrin saturation is serum iron divided by TIBC, the fraction of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron. An elevated value is the usual first screening clue to hemochromatosis.

TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) indirectly measures transferrin. It tends to be reduced in iron overload, the opposite of the high TIBC seen in iron deficiency, though not every patient shows this.

GI-025.detail: In hereditary hemochromatosis, excess iron deposits in parenchymal tissues. Arthropathy classically involves the second and third MCP joints with hook-like osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis. Islet damage causes diabetes, myocardial iron causes cardiomyopathy (dilated or restrictive) and arrhythmias, and pituitary iron causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Skin bronzing is another classic feature but is not used here.

Iron deposition in pancreatic islets impairs insulin secretion, the basis of 'bronze diabetes'.

Iron in the anterior pituitary reduces gonadotropins, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low libido, impotence, amenorrhea).

GI-026.detail: Excess body iron can be removed by phlebotomy or by chelating drugs that bind iron for excretion. Therapeutic phlebotomy is first-line for HFE hemochromatosis, because each unit of blood removes iron in hemoglobin. Chelators are mainly used for transfusional iron overload, as in thalassemia, or when phlebotomy is not suitable, such as in patients with anemia.

Deferasirox is an oral iron chelator used mainly for chronic transfusional iron overload. Its notable adverse effects include kidney and liver toxicity.
Deferiprone is an oral iron chelator used for transfusional iron overload, particularly in thalassemia. Agranulocytosis is its important adverse effect, requiring blood count monitoring.

GI-027.detail: The liver synthesizes clotting factors and albumin, maintains blood glucose and detoxifies ammonia, so advanced hepatocellular failure impairs all of these. PT/INR and albumin are standard measures of synthetic function and are part of prognostic scores such as Child-Pugh and MELD. In cirrhosis a prolonged INR reflects reduced synthesis rather than net bleeding risk, because anticoagulant proteins also fall; not every abnormality is present at once.
tileNotes: PT/INR measures the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. It is prolonged in liver failure because the liver makes most clotting factors, though it does not reliably predict bleeding in cirrhosis.
Albumin is the main plasma protein made by the liver and maintains oncotic pressure. Low levels in cirrhosis reflect reduced synthesis and contribute to edema and ascites.
Hypoglycemia is low blood glucose. It can occur in advanced liver failure because gluconeogenesis and glycogen storage are impaired.
Hyperammonemia is elevated blood ammonia. A failing liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, and portosystemic shunting adds to the problem; it contributes to hepatic encephalopathy.

GI-028.detail: In cirrhosis, reduced hepatic metabolism of estrogens and increased peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens shift the hormonal balance, along with reduced free testosterone. This hyperestrogenic state contributes to gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema and hypogonadism, although it is not the only mechanism for each finding. These peripheral stigmata are useful bedside clues to chronic liver disease.
tileNotes: Gynecomastia is benign enlargement of male breast glandular tissue. In cirrhosis it reflects a higher estrogen-to-androgen ratio.

Spider angiomas are small vascular lesions with a central arteriole and radiating vessels that blanch with pressure. They typically appear on the upper trunk and face and are associated with excess estrogen.
Palmar erythema is redness of the palms, especially the thenar and hypothenar eminences. It is a classic stigma of chronic liver disease linked in part to hyperestrogenism.

Hypogonadism in cirrhosis can present as testicular atrophy, reduced libido and menstrual irregularity. Altered sex-hormone metabolism contributes, though direct effects such as alcohol toxicity also play a role.

GI-029.detail: Portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, increases sinusoidal pressure and causes ascites, especially with hypoalbuminemia and renal sodium retention. Blood diverts through portosystemic anastomoses, dilating veins at the rectum (superior with middle/inferior rectal veins) and around the umbilicus (paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins). Back-pressure through the splenic vein causes congestive splenomegaly and hypersplenism. Anorectal varices are distinct from ordinary internal hemorrhoids.

Back-pressure through the splenic vein causes congestive splenomegaly, often with thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism.

history.detail: When portal venous pressure rises, blood is diverted through portosystemic collaterals that dilate into varices, and the spleen becomes congested. Esophageal varices are the most dangerous, since rupture can cause massive bleeding. Anorectal varices and caput medusae are other collateral pathways, and splenomegaly can cause hypersplenism with thrombocytopenia.

GI-030.detail: Portal hypertension is classified by where resistance to flow occurs: prehepatic, intrahepatic or posthepatic. Portal vein thrombosis is prehepatic, cirrhosis causes sinusoidal intrahepatic obstruction, schistosomiasis causes presinusoidal intrahepatic obstruction, and Budd-Chiari syndrome blocks hepatic venous outflow. The site matters for diagnosis because the hepatic venous pressure gradient is normal in prehepatic and presinusoidal causes but raised in sinusoidal disease such as cirrhosis.
tileNotes: Portal vein thrombosis is a clot in the portal vein, a prehepatic cause of portal hypertension. Liver function is often preserved because the hepatic parenchyma itself is not diseased.
Cirrhosis is diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules that distorts the hepatic architecture. It is the most common cause of portal hypertension and obstructs flow at the sinusoidal level.

Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection in which Schistosoma mansoni or japonicum eggs lodge in portal venules. The resulting granulomas and periportal fibrosis cause presinusoidal portal hypertension.

Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, often from thrombosis of the hepatic veins. It is a posthepatic cause and classically presents with abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites.
