GI-034.detail: Cholesterol gallstones form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol or when gallbladder emptying slows. Obesity and estrogen increase biliary cholesterol secretion, fibrates increase cholesterol excretion into bile, and rapid weight loss mobilizes cholesterol while reducing gallbladder motility. These are risk factors that increase likelihood rather than guaranteeing stone formation.
tileNotes: Obesity increases hepatic cholesterol synthesis and secretion into bile. This raises cholesterol saturation and promotes cholesterol stone formation.
Estrogen exposure, from pregnancy, oral contraceptives or hormone therapy, increases biliary cholesterol secretion. It helps explain the higher gallstone risk in women.
Fibrate use refers to lipid-lowering drugs such as gemfibrozil and fenofibrate. They increase biliary cholesterol excretion and can reduce bile acid synthesis, favoring cholesterol stones.
Rapid weight loss, as with very low calorie diets or bariatric surgery, mobilizes cholesterol into bile and reduces gallbladder emptying. Both effects favor stone formation.

GI-035.detail: When bile flow is impaired, conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and spills into the urine, while less bilirubin reaches the gut. The result is jaundice, dark urine and pale stools, often with itching from retained bile constituents. Pale stools generally indicate substantial or complete obstruction, and this cluster prompts imaging of the biliary tree.
tileNotes: Jaundice is yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae from elevated bilirubin. In cholestasis the excess bilirubin is mainly conjugated.
Dark urine results from conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble, being excreted by the kidneys. Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and does not appear in urine.
Pale stools, also called acholic stools, occur when little bilirubin reaches the intestine to be converted into stercobilin. They generally signal significant obstruction to bile flow.
Pruritus is itching. In cholestasis it is attributed to retained bile acids and other pruritogens and can be severe.

Antimitochondrial antibodies are the serologic hallmark, and biopsy can show the florid duct lesion with lymphocytic inflammation and granulomas. Portal-tract granulomas around damaged bile ducts form part of the florid duct lesion. When present on biopsy, they are a characteristic histologic clue to PBC.

Xanthelasma are yellowish cholesterol-rich plaques on the eyelids. In PBC they can reflect hypercholesterolemia from chronic cholestasis, but they also occur in other hyperlipidemic states and in people with normal lipids.

GI-039.detail: Beyond gallstones and alcohol, the most common causes, acute pancreatitis has several recognized metabolic, infectious and iatrogenic triggers. Severe hypertriglyceridemia and hypercalcemia are important metabolic causes, mumps is a classic viral cause, and ERCP can cause post-procedure pancreatitis. Calcium direction matters: hypercalcemia can cause pancreatitis, whereas hypocalcemia is a consequence and marker of severity.
tileNotes: Hypertriglyceridemia means elevated blood triglycerides. Very high levels, typically around 1000 mg/dL or more, can trigger acute pancreatitis.
Hypercalcemia is elevated serum calcium, for example from hyperparathyroidism. It can activate pancreatic enzymes within the gland and is a recognized cause of acute pancreatitis.
Mumps is a paramyxovirus infection best known for parotitis. It can also infect the pancreas and cause acute pancreatitis.
ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) is an endoscopic procedure to image and treat the bile and pancreatic ducts. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is its most common significant complication.

GI-042.detail: Advanced chronic pancreatitis destroys acinar tissue, leaving calcified ducts and an atrophic gland that secretes too little enzyme, which shows up as low fecal elastase. A normal D-xylose test points to intact small-bowel mucosa, helping separate pancreatic (maldigestion) from mucosal malabsorption, provided no coexisting mucosal disease is present. Calcifications and low elastase are typical of advanced disease but are not universal.

Atrophy means loss of glandular tissue, so the pancreas appears shrunken on imaging. Progressive fibrosis replaces acini in chronic pancreatitis, reducing enzyme output.
Elastase is a pancreatic enzyme that survives passage through the gut, so stool levels reflect pancreatic secretion. A low value supports exocrine insufficiency.
D-xylose is a sugar absorbed by the small-bowel mucosa without needing pancreatic enzymes. Normal absorption suggests the mucosa is intact, pointing the malabsorption toward a pancreatic cause.

GI-045.detail: Functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet-type cells and secrete a hormone in excess, so each produces a recognizable clinical syndrome. Insulinoma causes hypoglycemia, glucagonoma causes a rash with diabetes, VIPoma causes profuse watery diarrhea and somatostatinoma causes diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhea. Linking each tumor to its hormone and syndrome is a frequent exam task.
tileNotes: An insulin-secreting tumor arising from beta cells. It causes fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide levels.
A tumor of alpha cells that secretes glucagon. Its syndrome includes necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss and venous thrombosis.
A tumor secreting vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Excess VIP drives large-volume secretory diarrhea with hypokalemia and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome).
A tumor of delta cells that secretes somatostatin. Because somatostatin inhibits many hormones, it can cause diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhea.

GI-048.detail: Somatostatin broadly suppresses endocrine and exocrine secretion. Excess hormone inhibits insulin release (diabetes), cholecystokinin and gallbladder contraction (gallstones) and pancreatic enzyme secretion (steatorrhea), with weight loss accompanying the malabsorption. The diabetes, gallstone and steatorrhea triad is the distinctive pattern, since steatorrhea and weight loss alone occur in many GI disorders.
tileNotes: Somatostatin inhibits insulin secretion from beta cells. Excess hormone from a somatostatinoma therefore causes hyperglycemia and diabetes.
Cholelithiasis means gallstones. Somatostatin blocks cholecystokinin release and gallbladder contraction, so bile stagnates and stones form.
Steatorrhea is fatty, foul-smelling, floating stool from fat malabsorption. Somatostatin suppresses pancreatic enzyme secretion, impairing fat digestion.
Loss of body weight, here largely from malabsorption of fat and nutrients. It accompanies the triad but is nonspecific on its own.

GI-049.detail: Intestinal crypts are the regenerative base of the small-intestinal epithelium. Stem cells near the crypt base continuously renew the lining, Paneth cells sit beside them secreting antimicrobial products, and goblet and enteroendocrine cells are also present, though these two populate the villi as well. Knowing which cells are crypt-restricted is a common histology question.
tileNotes: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting epithelial cells with a cup-shaped appearance. They are found in crypts and also along the villi, where mucus protects and lubricates the surface.
Paneth cells are granule-filled cells at the crypt base that secrete antimicrobial products such as lysozyme and defensins. They are restricted to the crypts.
Intestinal stem cells reside in the lower crypt and divide to replace the epithelium every few days. They give rise to all the other epithelial cell types.
Enteroendocrine cells secrete hormones such as cholecystokinin, secretin and serotonin into the surrounding tissue. They occur in crypts and are also scattered along the villi.

GI-052.detail: Whipple disease is a systemic infection with Tropheryma whipplei, which is why it reaches far beyond the gut. Joint symptoms often precede gastrointestinal symptoms by years, and the organism can cause blood culture-negative endocarditis, lymphadenopathy and central nervous system involvement. Recognizing these extraintestinal features helps diagnose it when malabsorption is not yet prominent.

Enlargement of lymph nodes, which in Whipple disease can contain macrophages filled with the organism. Mesenteric and peripheral nodes can be involved.
Central nervous system involvement can cause cognitive change, eye movement abnormalities or other deficits. Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is a classic, highly suggestive sign of CNS Whipple disease.

GI-053.detail: Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive defect in MTP, which loads lipid onto ApoB-48 and ApoB-100. Without it, chylomicrons and VLDL cannot be assembled or secreted, so enterocytes fill with lipid and plasma ApoB lipoproteins are nearly absent. Abnormal red cell membrane lipids produce acanthocytes, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (especially vitamin E) causes retinitis pigmentosa and spinocerebellar degeneration. Infants present with steatorrhea and failure to thrive.

Cholera toxin and ETEC heat-labile toxin ADP-ribosylate Gs to lock it on, pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi to disable it, and anthrax edema factor is itself an adenylate cyclase. MICRO-005.detail: Clostridia are gram-positive, spore-forming, obligately anaerobic rods. Spores survive heat, drying and many disinfectants, which explains wound contamination from soil, foodborne botulism and the persistence of C. difficile on hospital surfaces. Because alcohol hand rubs do not reliably kill spores, soap and water handwashing is advised when caring for patients with C. difficile.

Clostridium botulinum forms heat-resistant spores found in soil and improperly preserved foods. Its neurotoxin blocks acetylcholine release, producing descending flaccid paralysis; infant botulism follows ingestion of spores, classically from honey.
Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene (myonecrosis) through alpha toxin, a lecithinase. Some strains also cause food poisoning when spores survive cooking of meat dishes.

Clostridioides difficile, renamed from Clostridium but phenotypically unchanged, is a spore-forming anaerobe. After antibiotics disrupt gut flora, its toxins A and B cause diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis.

Because these organisms lack a peptidoglycan cell wall (Mycoplasma) or live largely inside host cells, beta-lactams are ineffective and they stain poorly or not at all on routine Gram stain. MICRO-010.detail: Pasteurization kills many pathogens that can contaminate milk and soft cheeses, so unpasteurized dairy is a classic exposure clue. These organisms cause quite different illnesses, from invasive listeriosis and undulant fever to bacterial enteritis. Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative rod that grows in the cold and can contaminate pork and unpasteurized milk. It can cause enterocolitis or mesenteric adenitis that mimics appendicitis.

MICRO-012.detail: Tetanospasmin travels retrogradely to the spinal cord and blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA from inhibitory interneurons such as Renshaw cells. Unopposed motor activity produces rigidity and violent spasms, classically starting in the jaw. Not every patient shows every sign, but recognizing these findings prompts urgent antitoxin, wound care and airway support.
tileNotes: Trismus (lockjaw) is spasm of the masseter muscles that prevents opening the mouth. It is often the earliest and most recognizable sign of generalized tetanus.
Risus sardonicus is a fixed grimace from sustained facial muscle spasm, with raised eyebrows and drawn-back corners of the mouth. It reflects loss of inhibitory control over facial muscles.
Opisthotonos is severe arching of the back with the head and heels bent backward. It results from spasm of the powerful extensor muscles of the neck and back.
Generalized tetanic spasms are intensely painful and can be triggered by noise, touch or light. Spasm of laryngeal or respiratory muscles can threaten the airway and breathing.

MICRO-013.detail: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions and cholinergic autonomic synapses. Weakness classically begins in cranial nerve muscles (diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia) and descends symmetrically, accompanied by reduced reflexes and autonomic signs. Mental status and sensation are typically preserved, which helps separate botulism from other causes of acute weakness.
tileNotes: Botulism weakness usually starts in muscles served by cranial nerves, then spreads down to the arms, trunk, legs and respiratory muscles. This descending, symmetric pattern contrasts with the classic ascending weakness of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Hyporeflexia means diminished deep tendon reflexes. It follows from blocked neuromuscular transmission and fits the flaccid weakness of botulism.

Mydriasis is pupillary dilation. Blockade of parasympathetic cholinergic input to the iris sphincter leaves pupils dilated and poorly reactive, a feature that helps distinguish botulism from myasthenia gravis.
Xerostomia is dry mouth from reduced saliva. It reflects blockade of cholinergic parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, part of the autonomic picture of botulism.

MICRO-015.detail: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic gram-negative rod that thrives in moist environments and resists many disinfectants and antibiotics. These syndromes reflect classic exposures: warm water, diabetes or immunocompromise, contact lens wear and plantar puncture wounds through footwear. None is exclusively pseudomonal, but in the right setting each should raise suspicion for Pseudomonas when choosing therapy.

Osteomyelitis is infection of bone. A nail puncture through the sole of a sneaker is the classic scenario for Pseudomonas osteomyelitis or osteochondritis of the foot.

MICRO-016.detail: Late congenital syphilis reflects chronic Treponema pallidum inflammation of developing bone, cartilage, cornea, and the eighth cranial nerve. Classic stigmata include interstitial keratitis, eighth-nerve deafness, saber shins (anterior tibial bowing), saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, and mulberry molars. Early congenital syphilis (before age 2) instead features rhinitis (snuffles), rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and osteochondritis. Each tile has look-alike causes (Cogan syndrome for keratitis with deafness, granulomatosis with polyangiitis for saddle nose), so the shared link must be recognized as a set.

Saddle nose results from destruction of nasal cartilage and bone, a late facial stigma of congenital syphilis.
Eighth cranial nerve involvement causes sensorineural deafness, usually appearing in late childhood, and is part of the Hutchinson triad.

MICRO-017.detail: Bacterial vaginosis results from loss of protective lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes and Gardnerella vaginalis, with little true inflammation. The Amsel criteria provide a bedside diagnosis: at least three of the four findings are required, not all four. Gram stain scoring (Nugent) is a laboratory alternative, and metronidazole is a classic treatment.

In the whiff test, adding potassium hydroxide to discharge releases a fishy odor from amines produced by anaerobes. A positive result supports bacterial vaginosis, though trichomoniasis can also be positive.

MICRO-018.detail: These endemic fungi grow as molds in specific geographic soils and infect people who inhale airborne spores, so the lung is the usual first site. Many infections are mild or subclinical, but dissemination can occur, particularly with impaired cellular immunity. Travel and residence history is key: Histoplasma (Ohio and Mississippi river valleys), Blastomyces (eastern and central US), Coccidioides (southwestern US) and Paracoccidioides (Latin America).
tileNotes: Histoplasma capsulatum is linked to soil contaminated by bird or bat droppings, such as in caves. Inhaled spores convert to small yeasts that live inside macrophages and can disseminate in the immunocompromised.
Blastomyces dermatitidis appears in tissue as large yeast with broad-based budding. After inhalation it causes pneumonia and can spread to skin and bone.
Coccidioides species live in desert soil and are inhaled as arthroconidia, sometimes after dust storms or earthquakes. In tissue they form spherules filled with endospores rather than budding yeast.

Paracoccidioides species cause paracoccidioidomycosis in Latin America and appear in tissue as yeast with multiple buds (captain's wheel). Infection begins in the lungs and can involve the oral mucosa.

MICRO-030.detail: These four Plasmodium species form the classic teaching set for human malaria, transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. They differ in severity, the red cells they infect, fever periodicity and whether dormant liver forms persist. P. falciparum causes the most severe disease, while P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites that require primaquine or tafenoquine to prevent relapse. P. knowlesi is a recognized fifth human species.
tileNotes: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe malaria, with high parasitemia and infected red cells adhering to small vessels. Complications include cerebral malaria, severe anemia and renal failure; banana-shaped gametocytes are a classic smear finding.
Plasmodium vivax preferentially infects young red cells (reticulocytes) and classically causes fevers every 48 hours. Its dormant liver hypnozoites can reactivate and cause relapse months later.
Plasmodium ovale resembles vivax, with a 48-hour fever cycle and relapsing hypnozoites. Infected red cells may appear oval with fimbriated edges on a blood smear.
Plasmodium malariae causes a 72-hour (quartan) fever cycle and band forms on smear. It does not form hypnozoites but can persist at low levels for years and is associated with nephrotic syndrome.

MICRO-031.detail: Babesia is a protozoan that infects red blood cells; B. microti is classically transmitted by Ixodes ticks in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States, the same vector as Lyme disease. Parasites multiply as amastigotes in macrophages of the spleen, liver and bone marrow, producing fever, weight loss, marked hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. Pancytopenia is a reduction in red cells, white cells and platelets. In visceral leishmaniasis it results from marrow involvement and splenic sequestration, raising the risk of infection and bleeding.

Rotavirus is a reovirus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA. It is a major cause of severe watery diarrhea in infants and young children, and oral vaccines are available.

Ofloxacin is an older fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin is its active isomer) that inhibits gyrase and topoisomerase IV. It is commonly used as ear or eye drops.

MICRO-061.detail: Rifamycins inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription. Rifampin, rifabutin and rifapentine are absorbed systemically and used against mycobacteria, whereas rifaximin is minimally absorbed and acts within the gut. Rifampin is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP enzymes and rifabutin a weaker one, a difference that matters for drug interactions such as with HIV antiretrovirals.
tileNotes: Rifampin is the prototype rifamycin and a core TB drug, also used for latent TB and meningococcal prophylaxis. It strongly induces CYP enzymes and turns urine, tears and other body fluids red-orange.

Rifabutin is a systemic rifamycin used for mycobacterial infections. Because it induces CYP enzymes less than rifampin, it is often substituted in patients taking interacting drugs such as HIV protease inhibitors.
Rifapentine is a long-acting systemic rifamycin that allows less frequent dosing. It is used in some TB regimens, including once-weekly treatment of latent TB with isoniazid.
Rifaximin is a rifamycin that is minimally absorbed from the gut, so it acts locally. It is used for hepatic encephalopathy and travelers' diarrhea rather than for systemic infections.

MICRO-062.detail: Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol make up the classic four-drug initial (intensive) phase for drug-susceptible active tuberculosis, typically followed by a continuation phase with fewer drugs. Combination therapy limits the emergence of resistance. The exact regimen and duration depend on susceptibility, disease site, patient factors and current guidance, and this regimen is not the treatment for latent TB.
tileNotes: Rifampin inhibits mycobacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is a key sterilizing drug in RIPE. It induces CYP enzymes, causing many drug interactions, and harmlessly turns body fluids red-orange.

Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and requires activation by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG). Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy are classic toxicities, and pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given to prevent neuropathy.
Pyrazinamide is active against mycobacteria in acidic environments such as within macrophages. It is used in the initial phase and can cause hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia.

Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase, impairing synthesis of mycobacterial cell-wall arabinogalactan. Its classic toxicity is optic neuritis, which can present as reduced acuity or red-green color vision loss.

MICRO-063.detail: These triazoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the main sterol of fungal cell membranes. Many also inhibit human CYP enzymes to varying degrees, so drug interactions are common. Spectrum, pharmacokinetics and toxicity differ by agent, and isavuconazole is an additional member of the class.
tileNotes: Fluconazole is a water-soluble triazole with good CSF penetration. It is used for many Candida infections and in cryptococcal meningitis therapy, but it has no useful activity against Aspergillus.

Itraconazole is a triazole used for endemic mycoses such as histoplasmosis and blastomycosis and for some nail infections. Its negative inotropic effect means it is generally avoided in heart failure.
Voriconazole is a triazole that is a first-line agent for invasive aspergillosis. Notable adverse effects include transient visual disturbances, photosensitivity and hepatotoxicity.

Posaconazole is a broad-spectrum triazole that also has activity against many Mucorales. It is used for antifungal prophylaxis in high-risk hematologic patients and as step-down or salvage therapy for mucormycosis.

MICRO-065.detail: Integrase strand-transfer inhibitors block HIV integrase from inserting viral DNA into the host chromosome, a step required for stable infection of the cell. They are used as part of combination antiretroviral regimens, not as monotherapy. Elvitegravir requires pharmacokinetic boosting, typically with cobicistat, whereas the others do not, and as a class they are chelated by antacids and other polyvalent cations.
tileNotes: Bictegravir is a second-generation INSTI given in a fixed-dose combination with two NRTIs as a single daily tablet. It does not require a pharmacokinetic booster.

Dolutegravir is a second-generation INSTI with a relatively high barrier to resistance, used in many first-line regimens. Like other INSTIs, it should be separated from antacids and supplements containing polyvalent cations.
Elvitegravir is an INSTI that must be pharmacokinetically boosted, usually with cobicistat, to reach adequate levels. The booster adds CYP3A-mediated drug interactions not seen with unboosted INSTIs.
Raltegravir was the first INSTI approved. It is unboosted and has been associated with creatine kinase elevation and myopathy in some patients.

MICRO-066.detail: NNRTIs bind a hydrophobic pocket on HIV-1 reverse transcriptase near the active site, changing its shape allosterically. Unlike nucleoside analogues, they do not need intracellular phosphorylation and do not compete with nucleotides. HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to the class, and each agent has its own interaction and toxicity profile.
tileNotes: Efavirenz is an older NNRTI known for neuropsychiatric effects such as vivid dreams and dizziness. It is a CYP inducer and can cause rash.

Nevirapine is an older NNRTI whose classic toxicities are severe hepatotoxicity and serious rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Like the rest of the class, it inhibits reverse transcriptase allosterically without needing phosphorylation.
Doravirine is a newer NNRTI with fewer neuropsychiatric effects than efavirenz. It shares the class mechanism of allosteric reverse-transcriptase inhibition and is used in combination regimens.

Rilpivirine is a newer NNRTI that needs gastric acid for absorption, so proton pump inhibitors are contraindicated with the oral form. It is available in combination tablets and as a long-acting injectable with cabotegravir.

MICRO-067.detail: These NRTIs are nucleoside analogues that must be phosphorylated inside the cell to their active triphosphate form. Lacking a 3'-hydroxyl group, they terminate the growing DNA chain when incorporated by reverse transcriptase. They differ in resistance, toxicity and anti-hepatitis B activity, with lamivudine and emtricitabine also active against HBV.
tileNotes: Abacavir is a guanosine analogue NRTI. Testing for HLA-B*57:01 is required before use because carriers are at high risk of a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction.
Lamivudine (3TC) is a cytidine analogue NRTI that is generally well tolerated. It is also active against hepatitis B, and the single M184V mutation can confer high-level resistance.

Emtricitabine (FTC) is a cytidine analogue closely related to lamivudine that shares its M184V resistance pathway. It is active against hepatitis B and is a common backbone component of combination tablets.

Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine analogue and was the first approved antiretroviral. Bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia) is its classic toxicity, and it has been used to prevent perinatal transmission.

MICRO-068.detail: HIV protease cleaves the gag and gag-pol polyproteins into functional proteins, a step needed for virions to mature and become infectious. Protease inhibitors block this step, leaving immature, noninfectious particles. Ritonavir is now mainly used at low dose to inhibit CYP3A4 and boost other protease inhibitors, though it remains a protease inhibitor itself, and these agents are not all equally common in current regimens.
tileNotes: Atazanavir is a protease inhibitor that inhibits UGT1A1, often causing benign indirect hyperbilirubinemia and sometimes visible jaundice. Its absorption depends on gastric acid.
Lopinavir is a protease inhibitor co-formulated with low-dose ritonavir, which raises its blood levels. It is an older agent that can cause gastrointestinal effects and dyslipidemia.
Indinavir is an older protease inhibitor classically associated with nephrolithiasis and crystalluria. Generous hydration was required during therapy, and it is now rarely used.

Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor now used mainly at low dose as a booster, because it potently inhibits CYP3A4 and raises levels of co-administered drugs. This also makes it a major source of drug interactions.

MSK-002.detail: The spondyloarthritides are inflammatory arthritides that typically lack rheumatoid factor (hence 'seronegative') and share enthesitis, inflammatory back pain or sacroiliitis, peripheral arthritis and extra-articular features such as anterior uveitis. They are associated with HLA-B27, but the strength of the association varies by disease and phenotype, and a negative HLA-B27 does not exclude the diagnosis.
tileNotes: Ankylosing spondylitis is chronic inflammation mainly of the sacroiliac joints and spine, with morning stiffness that improves with exercise. Advanced disease can fuse the spine ('bamboo spine'), and it has the strongest HLA-B27 link of the group.

Psoriatic arthritis is inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis that can involve DIP joints and cause dactylitis ('sausage digits') and nail pitting. Axial involvement occurs in a subset of patients.

Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that follows a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection. It can present with arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis and classically affects lower-limb joints.

Enteropathic spondyloarthritis is the arthritis seen with Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis. Peripheral arthritis often parallels bowel activity, whereas axial disease tends to run an independent course.

MSK-003.detail: Reactive arthritis is a sterile, immune-mediated arthritis that develops after an infection elsewhere, typically within weeks; the organism is not found in the joint. Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella and Yersinia are the classic enteric triggers, while Chlamydia trachomatis is the classic genitourinary trigger. The list is not exhaustive, and HLA-B27 positive individuals are at higher risk.
tileNotes: Campylobacter jejuni is a curved gram-negative rod and a common cause of bloody diarrhea, often from undercooked poultry. Besides reactive arthritis, it is a classic antecedent of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Nontyphoidal Salmonella species are gram-negative rods that cause gastroenteritis, often linked to poultry, eggs or reptiles. Reactive arthritis can follow the diarrheal illness.
Shigella is a gram-negative rod that causes dysentery with bloody diarrhea and spreads with a very low infectious dose. Reactive arthritis is a recognized post-infectious complication.
Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative enteric pathogen that can cause diarrhea or pseudoappendicitis from mesenteric adenitis. It is a classic trigger of reactive arthritis.

MSK-004.detail: Thiazides cause volume contraction and compete with urate for tubular secretion, increasing proximal reabsorption. Pyrazinamide's metabolite pyrazinoic acid stimulates urate reabsorption via URAT1. Low-dose salicylate reduces urate excretion, while high doses are uricosuric. Niacin competes for renal urate excretion. Other drugs with this effect include loop diuretics, ethambutol, and cyclosporine; contrast drugs that lower urate, such as probenecid, losartan, and allopurinol.
tileNotes: Thiazides raise serum urate through volume contraction and competition with urate for proximal tubular secretion.
Pyrazinamide's metabolite pyrazinoic acid promotes renal urate reabsorption, so hyperuricemia is common during tuberculosis treatment.
Low-dose aspirin reduces renal urate excretion and raises serum urate; high doses have the opposite, uricosuric effect.
Niacin (nicotinic acid) reduces renal urate excretion and can precipitate gout attacks.

MSK-005.detail: Osteoarthritis is degeneration of articular cartilage with reactive remodeling of the adjacent bone. On radiographs this produces nonuniform joint-space narrowing (often worst in the weight-bearing compartment), subchondral sclerosis, marginal osteophytes and subchondral cysts. These findings are supportive rather than individually specific, and they contrast with rheumatoid arthritis, which shows uniform joint-space loss, periarticular osteopenia and erosions.
tileNotes: Joint-space narrowing on x-ray reflects cartilage loss. In osteoarthritis it is typically asymmetric within the joint, for example favoring the medial compartment of the knee, unlike the uniform narrowing of inflammatory arthritis.
Subchondral sclerosis is increased bone density just beneath the cartilage, seen as whitening on x-ray. It develops as exposed bone remodels under abnormal load (eburnation in its extreme form).
Osteophytes are bony spurs that form at joint margins as a reparative response to cartilage damage. In the fingers they produce Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes.
Subchondral cysts (geodes) are lucent cavities in the bone beneath damaged cartilage. They are thought to form as synovial fluid is forced into bone through cartilage defects.

MSK-007.detail: Osteopetrosis is a group of inherited disorders in which osteoclasts fail to resorb bone, for example because of carbonic anhydrase II deficiency or other defects that impair acidification. Bone becomes dense but brittle, foramina narrow and marrow space is lost, so fractures, cranial nerve palsies and cytopenias can result. tileNotes: Although it looks dense on x-ray, osteopetrotic bone is structurally abnormal and brittle. Pathologic fractures are a common presentation, particularly in the adult form.
Failure to remodel the skull narrows the foramina through which cranial nerves pass. Compression can cause vision loss (optic nerve), hearing loss or facial palsy.

Pancytopenia is reduction of red cells, white cells and platelets. In osteopetrosis, overgrown bone crowds out the marrow cavity, causing anemia, infections and bleeding, most prominently in the infantile form.
Extramedullary hematopoiesis is blood cell production outside the marrow, mainly in the liver and spleen. In osteopetrosis it compensates for lost marrow space and can produce hepatosplenomegaly.

MSK-009.detail: Paget disease of bone is localized, disordered remodeling: excessive osteoclastic resorption followed by chaotic osteoblastic formation, producing enlarged, thickened but weak bone. Skull involvement can enlarge the head and contribute to hearing loss, and extensive hypervascular bone can uncommonly drive high-output heart failure. Osteosarcoma is a rare late complication; serum alkaline phosphatase is typically elevated while calcium and phosphate are usually normal.
tileNotes: An increasing hat size reflects skull enlargement from thickened pagetic bone. It is a classic historical clue, and skull involvement may show patchy 'cotton wool' areas on x-ray.

High-output heart failure occurs when the heart cannot meet an abnormally high demand for blood flow. Extensive, highly vascular pagetic bone acts like arteriovenous shunting, but this complication is uncommon.
Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone-forming tumor. Arising in pagetic bone, it is a rare late complication in older adults, and new or worsening bone pain should raise concern.

MSK-010.detail: Conventional synthetic DMARDs slow joint damage in rheumatoid arthritis rather than only relieving symptoms, and methotrexate is the usual first-line anchor drug. They are distinct from NSAIDs, which treat symptoms only, from biologic DMARDs such as anti-TNF agents, and from targeted synthetic DMARDs such as JAK inhibitors. Onset of benefit is slow, often weeks to months, and monitoring needs differ by agent.

Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial used as a milder DMARD, often in combination therapy and in lupus. Retinal toxicity is its key long-term risk, so periodic eye screening is needed.

Sulfasalazine combines sulfapyridine with 5-aminosalicylic acid and is used in RA and inflammatory bowel disease. It can cause gastrointestinal upset, rash, reversible oligospermia and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

Leflunomide inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in activated lymphocytes. It is hepatotoxic and teratogenic, and its long half-life may require a cholestyramine washout.

MSK-025.detail: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel at the elbow, then through Guyon canal beside the hook of hamate at the wrist. Injury at either level weakens the intrinsic hand muscles and, in chronic lesions, can cause clawing of the fourth and fifth digits. Deficits depend on the level: dorsal hand sensation is usually spared in Guyon canal lesions because the dorsal cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist.
tileNotes: The hook of hamate is a bony projection on the palmar wrist that forms the lateral wall of Guyon canal. Fractures, classically from gripping a bat, club or racquet, can injure the adjacent ulnar nerve.

The medial epicondyle is the bony prominence on the inner distal humerus, behind which the ulnar nerve runs. Fractures here, more common in children and adolescents, can injure the nerve at the elbow.

Guyon canal (the ulnar canal) is a tunnel at the wrist between the pisiform and the hook of hamate. Compression there, for example from prolonged handlebar pressure in cyclists, affects the hand intrinsics but usually spares dorsal hand sensation.

MSK-030.detail: The four principal knee ligaments provide passive stability in two planes. The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments prevent anterior and posterior translation of the tibia on the femur, while the medial and lateral collateral ligaments resist valgus and varus stress. Exams commonly test the matching examination maneuvers and injury mechanisms, such as the 'unhappy triad' of ACL, MCL and meniscal injury.

The medial collateral ligament spans the inner knee from femur to tibia and resists valgus (outward-angling) stress. It is injured by a blow to the lateral knee and tested with a valgus stress test.
The lateral collateral ligament runs from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head and resists varus stress. It is injured by a blow to the medial knee and tested with a varus stress test.

MSK-032.detail: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) is death of bone and marrow from impaired blood supply, classically affecting the femoral head and causing groin or hip pain. Glucocorticoid exposure, heavy alcohol use, Gaucher disease and decompression sickness are nontraumatic risk settings that compromise marrow microcirculation, for example through altered marrow fat, cellular infiltration or gas bubbles. They raise risk but do not invariably cause osteonecrosis, and MRI is the most sensitive early imaging test.

Decompression sickness occurs when dissolved nitrogen forms gas bubbles during too-rapid ascent, as in divers. The bubbles can occlude bone microvasculature, causing dysbaric osteonecrosis.

MSK-033.detail: Acute compartment syndrome occurs when pressure inside a closed fascial compartment rises enough to impair capillary perfusion, causing ischemic injury to muscle and nerve. Fracture is the most common cause, but burns, reperfusion after ischemia and envenomation can also raise compartment pressure. Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch are early clues; palpable pulses do not exclude the diagnosis, and treatment is urgent fasciotomy.
tileNotes: Fractures, especially of the tibial shaft and forearm, are the most common cause of acute compartment syndrome. Bleeding and swelling within the compartment raise pressure inside the unyielding fascia.

Burns cause marked capillary leak and tissue edema, and circumferential full-thickness burns form a rigid eschar. Together these can raise compartment pressure, sometimes requiring escharotomy or fasciotomy.

Reperfusion injury occurs when blood flow returns to previously ischemic tissue, triggering free radical damage and capillary leak. The resulting swelling, for example after vascular repair, can precipitate compartment syndrome.
Envenomation is injection of venom, as from certain snake bites. Local tissue injury and swelling can raise compartment pressure, so compartments may need close monitoring.

MSK-034.detail: The Ottawa ankle and foot rules help decide which patients with acute ankle or midfoot injuries need radiographs, reducing unnecessary imaging. Imaging is indicated when there is pain in the malleolar or midfoot zone plus either bony tenderness at one of these landmarks or inability to bear weight for four steps, both immediately and at evaluation. The landmarks are only part of the rule, which also has age and exclusion criteria.

The base of the fifth metatarsal is the bony prominence on the outer midfoot where peroneus brevis inserts. Tenderness here is an Ottawa foot criterion and can indicate an avulsion or Jones fracture.
The navicular is a midfoot bone on the inner side of the foot, just in front of the talus. Tenderness over it is an Ottawa foot criterion for radiographs.

MSK-035.detail: Stress fractures result from repetitive loading that outpaces bone repair. At high-risk sites, tensile forces or poor blood supply raise the risk of displacement, nonunion or avascular necrosis, so these injuries need location-specific and often surgical management rather than simple rest. The tension (superolateral) side of the femoral neck and the anterior tibial cortex, where a 'dreaded black line' may be seen, are classic high-risk tension-side lesions.
tileNotes: Femoral neck stress fractures on the tension (superolateral) side tend to progress to complete, displaced fracture. Displacement threatens the femoral head blood supply, so these usually need surgical fixation.

The anterior tibial cortex lies on the tension side of the tibia and has relatively poor blood supply. Stress fractures here heal slowly, may show a 'dreaded black line' on lateral radiographs and can progress to complete fracture.

The talus is the ankle bone linking the leg to the foot, with an extensive cartilage surface and a vulnerable blood supply. Stress fractures here are considered high risk because of delayed healing and possible avascular necrosis.

Stress fractures of the proximal fifth metatarsal near the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (the Jones region) occur in a watershed area of blood supply. They are prone to delayed union and nonunion and are often treated surgically in athletes.

MSK-036.detail: These NSAIDs reversibly inhibit COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and producing analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects. Aspirin is the classic contrast because it irreversibly acetylates COX, which is why its antiplatelet effect lasts for the life of the platelet. Shared adverse effects include gastrointestinal ulceration, kidney injury from loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation, and fluid retention.
tileNotes: Ibuprofen is a widely used nonselective NSAID for pain, fever and inflammation. Its COX inhibition is reversible, and taking it before aspirin can interfere with aspirin's antiplatelet effect.
Naproxen is a nonselective NSAID with a longer half-life than ibuprofen, allowing twice-daily dosing. It is commonly used for musculoskeletal pain and acute gout flares.
Indomethacin is a potent nonselective NSAID used for acute gout and some headache syndromes. By reducing PGE2, it is also used to close a patent ductus arteriosus in neonates.

Diclofenac is a nonselective NSAID available in oral and topical forms, often used for musculoskeletal pain. Like other reversible NSAIDs it can cause gastrointestinal and renal toxicity, and it has been associated with hepatotoxicity.

MSK-037.detail: Urate-lowering therapy reduces serum urate to prevent future gout flares, tophi and joint damage. Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase to reduce urate production, probenecid increases renal urate excretion, and pegloticase converts urate to soluble allantoin and is reserved for refractory disease. These drugs do not relieve an acute flare, which is treated with colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids, and starting therapy can transiently provoke flares.

Febuxostat is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces urate production. It is an alternative to allopurinol but carries a warning about increased cardiovascular death in patients with established cardiovascular disease.
Probenecid is a uricosuric drug that inhibits urate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. It is less effective when kidney function is reduced and can promote uric acid kidney stones.

Pegloticase is an intravenous recombinant uricase that converts urate to allantoin, which is readily excreted. It is reserved for refractory gout and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because of the risk of hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

MSK-038.detail: Bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogues that bind bone mineral and are taken up by osteoclasts; nitrogen-containing agents inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, impairing osteoclast function and survival. They are used for osteoporosis, Paget disease and hypercalcemia of malignancy. Agents differ in route, dosing and fracture-prevention evidence, and rare adverse effects include osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures.

Risedronate is an oral nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and Paget disease. Like alendronate, it requires careful administration to limit esophageal irritation.

Zoledronic acid is a potent intravenous bisphosphonate given yearly for osteoporosis, or more often for hypercalcemia of malignancy and bone metastases. An acute-phase reaction with fever and myalgias can follow the infusion.

Cyclooxygenase produces the prostanoids (prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane), while 5-lipoxygenase produces leukotrienes. MSK-041.detail: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder, most often due to RYR1 mutations, in which volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine trigger uncontrolled calcium release from the skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. Sustained contraction and hypermetabolism raise CO2 and lactate and break down muscle, releasing potassium and myoglobin. Rising end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign and hyperthermia may be late; none of these abnormalities is unique to MH, and dantrolene is the specific treatment.
tileNotes: Hypercapnia is an elevated blood CO2 level. In malignant hyperthermia, hypermetabolic muscle produces CO2 faster than ventilation clears it, and an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign.

Lactic acidosis is metabolic acidosis from lactate accumulation. Here oxygen demand outstrips supply in hypermetabolic muscle, shifting it toward anaerobic metabolism; with hypercapnia, this produces a mixed acidosis.
Hyperkalemia is a high serum potassium level that can cause dangerous arrhythmias. In malignant hyperthermia, damaged muscle cells release their intracellular potassium.
Rhabdomyolysis is breakdown of skeletal muscle that releases creatine kinase and myoglobin into the blood. Myoglobinuria can cause dark urine and acute kidney injury.

NEPH-001.detail: The definitive kidney (metanephros) develops from two interacting components: the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme. The ureteric bud, an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct, branches repeatedly to form the collecting system: collecting ducts, minor and major calyces, renal pelvis and ureter. Nephron segments arise separately from the metanephric mesenchyme, and failure of bud-mesenchyme interaction can cause renal agenesis.
tileNotes: Collecting ducts are the final tubular segments, adjusting water and sodium reabsorption under ADH and aldosterone. They are the most distal structures formed by the ureteric bud, where it joins the nephron.
Renal calyces are cup-shaped chambers that collect urine from the renal papillae, with minor calyces draining into major calyces. They form from early branching generations of the ureteric bud.
The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped chamber where the major calyces join before draining into the ureter. It forms from the expanded upper end of the ureteric bud.
The ureters are muscular tubes carrying urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. Each forms from the stalk of the ureteric bud, and abnormal budding can produce a duplicated ureter.

NEPH-002.detail: The metanephric mesenchyme (metanephric blastema) is induced by the ureteric bud to form nephrons, the kidney's functional filtering units. It gives rise to the nephron from the glomerulus through the distal convoluted tubule, including Bowman capsule, the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle. The collecting duct, by contrast, derives from the ureteric bud, a lineage boundary that is a classic exam distinction.
tileNotes: Glomeruli are capillary tufts enclosed by Bowman capsule, where blood is filtered to begin urine formation. Their epithelial components, including podocytes and Bowman capsule, develop from the metanephric mesenchyme.
The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most filtered sodium, water, glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. It forms from the metanephric mesenchyme as part of the developing nephron.
Loops of Henle dip into the medulla and set up the medullary concentration gradient, with NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. They are nephron segments derived from the metanephric mesenchyme.

The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium via the Na-Cl cotransporter and regulates calcium reabsorption under PTH. It is the last segment derived from the metanephric mesenchyme before the nephron joins a collecting duct.

NEPH-003.detail: Loop diuretics inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) on the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb, where a large share of filtered sodium is reabsorbed, making them the most potent diuretics in common use. Blocking NKCC2 also abolishes the lumen-positive potential that drives calcium and magnesium reabsorption, so they increase urinary calcium loss. Key adverse effects include hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, volume depletion and ototoxicity.
tileNotes: Furosemide is the prototype loop diuretic, used for edema from heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome. It is a sulfonamide derivative, and ototoxicity is a concern at high doses or with aminoglycosides.
Torsemide is a loop diuretic with more consistent oral absorption and a longer half-life than furosemide. It shares the class mechanism of NKCC2 inhibition in the thick ascending limb.
Bumetanide is a potent loop diuretic, effective at much lower milligram doses than furosemide. It acts on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and shares the class risks of hypokalemia and ototoxicity.
Ethacrynic acid is a loop diuretic that is not a sulfonamide, so it can be used in patients with sulfa allergy. It carries a higher risk of ototoxicity than other loop agents.

NEPH-005.detail: Potassium-sparing diuretics act in the late distal tubule and collecting duct, where aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption through ENaC and potassium secretion. Spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor, while amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly; both mechanisms cause weak natriuresis with potassium retention. Hyperkalemia, sometimes with metabolic acidosis, is the key risk, and the heart-failure mortality benefit applies only to the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
tileNotes: Spironolactone is a competitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist used for heart failure, primary hyperaldosteronism and ascites. It also blocks androgen receptors, which can cause gynecomastia.
Eplerenone is a more selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with fewer antiandrogen effects than spironolactone. It reduces mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct, independent of aldosterone. It is used in Liddle syndrome and for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Triamterene is an ENaC blocker often combined with hydrochlorothiazide to offset potassium loss. It is a recognized, though uncommon, cause of kidney stones.

NEPH-007.detail: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day in adults, which causes hypoalbuminemia and edema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis, causing hyperlipidemia and lipiduria. Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III, together with increased hepatic clotting factor synthesis, causes a hypercoagulable state with risk of renal vein thrombosis and other venous thromboembolism. Nephritic syndrome instead features hematuria, hypertension, and RBC casts with less proteinuria.

Urinary albumin loss exceeds hepatic synthesis, causing hypoalbuminemia.
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure and renal sodium retention cause edema, often periorbital at first.
The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, causing hyperlipidemia.

history.detail: Nephrotic syndrome results from podocyte or glomerular basement membrane injury that allows heavy urinary protein loss. Low serum albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure and, together with renal sodium retention, contributes to edema, while increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causes hyperlipidemia. In adults, nephrotic-range proteinuria is typically above 3.5 g/day, and patients are also at increased risk of thrombosis and infection.

Edema is swelling from excess interstitial fluid, often periorbital in children and dependent in adults. In nephrotic syndrome it reflects low oncotic pressure combined with renal sodium retention.

NEPH-008.detail: Minimal change disease is named for its nearly normal appearance on light microscopy, with no immune deposits on immunofluorescence. Electron microscopy reveals diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement, and proteinuria tends to be selective for albumin, especially in children. Effacement alone is nonspecific (it also occurs in FSGS), so the combined pattern points to the diagnosis. Minimal change disease is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
tileNotes: Light microscopy is the standard first look at a kidney biopsy. In minimal change disease the glomeruli look essentially normal, which is why the disease carries its name.

Podocytes are epithelial cells whose interdigitating foot processes form part of the filtration barrier. Electron microscopy shows these processes flattened (effaced), a key but nonspecific finding also seen in FSGS.
Immunofluorescence stains biopsy tissue for immunoglobulins and complement. A negative result argues against immune-complex glomerular diseases and fits minimal change disease.

Selective proteinuria means the urine protein is mostly albumin rather than larger proteins. This selectivity is typical of minimal change disease, particularly in children, and less consistent in adults.

NEPH-009.detail: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis can be primary or secondary to identifiable conditions. HIV and interferon therapy classically produce the collapsing variant, sickle cell disease causes FSGS through hyperfiltration, and heroin-associated FSGS is a historical association likely confounded by adulterants. Recognizing secondary causes matters because management targets the underlying driver rather than relying on immunosuppression alone.
tileNotes: HIV-associated nephropathy classically presents as a collapsing variant of FSGS with heavy proteinuria. It is a well-known secondary cause on exams.
Heroin nephropathy is a historical association with FSGS. Contaminants mixed into street heroin may have contributed, so the link is considered confounded.
Interferon is a cytokine used therapeutically for conditions such as viral hepatitis and multiple sclerosis. Like HIV, it is classically associated with the collapsing form of FSGS.
Sickle cell disease is an inherited hemoglobinopathy that affects many organs. In the kidney, glomerular hyperfiltration is thought to drive a secondary FSGS lesion.

NEPH-011.detail: Membranous nephropathy is defined by immune deposits beneath the podocyte (subepithelial), which thicken the capillary wall and produce granular staining along capillary loops on immunofluorescence. Anti-PLA2R antibodies identify the most common primary subtype but are not present in every case. Granular IgG and C3 staining also occurs in other immune-complex glomerulonephritides, so the features are most useful together.

NEPH-012.detail: PSGN follows pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A streptococcus, after a latent period of about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo. IgA nephropathy also causes cola-colored urine, but it occurs during or within days of infection and has normal C3 with mesangial IgA deposits.

NEPH-013.detail: Alport syndrome results from mutations in type IV collagen genes (COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5), a collagen shared by the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea and lens capsule. Persistent hematuria is the typical renal presentation, while hearing loss and ocular findings depend on genotype, age and sex and are most consistent in X-linked males. Electron microscopy may show a split, basket-weave basement membrane.
tileNotes: Hematuria is blood in the urine, often microscopic. Persistent hematuria from childhood is the typical first renal sign of Alport syndrome and may progress to proteinuria and kidney failure.
Sensorineural hearing loss arises from the inner ear or auditory nerve. In Alport syndrome it reflects abnormal type IV collagen in the cochlea and is not present in every patient.
Anterior lenticonus is a conical forward bulging of the lens surface due to a weakened lens capsule. It is a highly specific ocular clue to Alport syndrome.
Electron microscopy may show irregular thickening, thinning and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane. This lamellated appearance is described as basket-weave.

NEPH-016.detail: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form when urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus split urea into ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and promoting precipitation. They can grow into large staghorn calculi filling the renal pelvis and calyces. Not every struvite stone is staghorn and not every staghorn is struvite (cystine and uric acid can also form them), and treatment requires clearing both stone and infection.
tileNotes: Urease is a bacterial enzyme that hydrolyzes urea to ammonia. Organisms such as Proteus and Klebsiella produce it and create the chemical setting for struvite formation.
Ammonia from urea splitting raises urinary pH. Alkaline urine favors magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitation, although a high pH by itself is not specific for struvite.
Struvite crystals are classically described as rectangular prisms resembling coffin lids on urine microscopy. Their presence supports a struvite stone process.
A staghorn calculus is a branched stone that fills the renal pelvis and extends into calyces. Struvite is the classic cause, but cystine and uric acid stones can also take this shape.

NEPH-017.detail: Calcium oxalate is the most common kidney stone type, and risk rises when urinary oxalate increases or protective citrate falls. Ethylene glycol is metabolized to oxalate, excess vitamin C is converted to oxalate, and fat malabsorption leaves calcium bound to fat so more free oxalate is absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria). Ethylene glycol often causes acute crystal nephropathy rather than typical stone colic.
tileNotes: Ethylene glycol is a toxic alcohol found in antifreeze. Its metabolism produces oxalate, which can deposit as calcium oxalate crystals in the kidney and cause acute injury rather than classic colic.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is partly metabolized to oxalate. High supplemental intake can raise urinary oxalate and increase calcium oxalate stone risk.
Fat malabsorption occurs in conditions such as Crohn disease or after bowel resection. Unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria).
Citrate in the urine binds calcium and inhibits crystal formation. Low urinary citrate removes this protection, favoring calcium oxalate as well as calcium phosphate stones.

Aminoglycosides, cisplatin and amphotericin B are drug toxins, while myoglobin is an endogenous pigment released in rhabdomyolysis. Amphotericin B additionally causes afferent vasoconstriction and distal electrolyte wasting. Recognizing these exposures prompts dose adjustment, monitoring and hydration strategies.

NEPH-026.detail: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, reducing aqueous humor and cerebrospinal fluid production and increasing renal bicarbonate excretion. NEU-005.detail: Motor nuclei tend to lie near the midline of the brainstem, while sensory nuclei lie more laterally. The general somatic efferent nuclei of the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens and hypoglossal nerves follow this rule, which is why medial brainstem lesions can produce these cranial nerve palsies. The same four are also the pure somatic motor cranial nerves, so nucleus location is the key to the localization pattern.
tileNotes: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) has its somatic motor nucleus in the midbrain near the midline. It supplies most extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris.
The trochlear nerve (CN IV) nucleus sits medially in the caudal midbrain. It supplies the superior oblique muscle and is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem.
The abducens nerve (CN VI) nucleus lies near the midline in the dorsal pons beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. It supplies the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) nucleus lies close to the midline in the medulla. It supplies the tongue muscles, and a lesion causes the tongue to deviate toward the weak side on protrusion.

Optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia from MLF demyelination, heat-induced worsening (Uhthoff phenomenon) and Lhermitte sign are classic clinical clues. None is individually specific, but bilateral INO in a young adult is particularly suggestive. Diagnosis combines clinical features with MRI and sometimes CSF findings.
tileNotes: Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve, typically causing painful, usually unilateral vision loss with impaired color vision. It is a common initial presentation of MS.
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, not CN III. The adducting eye fails on lateral gaze while the abducting eye shows nystagmus.
Uhthoff phenomenon is temporary worsening of neurological symptoms with raised body temperature, such as exercise or a hot bath. Heat slows conduction in demyelinated axons.
Lhermitte sign is an electric sensation running down the spine or limbs on neck flexion. It suggests a cervical cord lesion and occurs in MS and other myelopathies.

NEU-013.detail: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC virus, which destroys oligodendrocytes in immunosuppressed patients. Risk settings include advanced HIV and drugs such as natalizumab, though most exposed patients do not develop it. MRI classically shows nonenhancing white matter lesions, but enhancement can occur, especially with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Restoring immune function is the main management approach.
tileNotes: JC virus is a polyomavirus that commonly establishes latent infection. In immunosuppressed hosts it can reactivate and infect the brain, causing PML.
Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in the central nervous system. JC virus infects and destroys them, causing demyelination; infected nuclei can appear enlarged on histology.

Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody against alpha-4 integrin used in multiple sclerosis and Crohn disease. It is a recognized risk for PML, so patients are monitored, often with JC virus antibody testing.
On MRI, PML typically shows asymmetric white matter lesions without contrast enhancement or mass effect. Enhancement can appear, particularly with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

NEU-014.detail: GABA-A and glycine receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels; opening them usually hyperpolarizes neurons and produces inhibition. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are positive allosteric modulators at the GABA-A receptor: benzodiazepines increase how often the channel opens, while barbiturates prolong opening. This shared mechanism explains their sedative, anxiolytic and anticonvulsant effects and the risk of respiratory depression when combined with other depressants.
tileNotes: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain. At the GABA-A receptor it opens a chloride channel, whereas GABA-B is a G protein-coupled receptor rather than a chloride channel.
Glycine is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem. Its receptor is a chloride channel, and strychnine blocks it, causing convulsions.
Benzodiazepines such as diazepam enhance GABA-A activity by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. They modulate the receptor rather than acting as direct agonists.
Barbiturates such as phenobarbital enhance GABA-A activity by increasing the duration of chloride channel opening. At high doses they can open the channel directly, increasing toxicity.

NEU-015.detail: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitors block breakdown of acetylcholine, increasing its action at synapses. Members of this class differ in site and use: edrophonium is very short acting and was historically used to test for myasthenia gravis, physostigmine enters the CNS and reverses anticholinergic toxicity, pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis peripherally, and donepezil treats Alzheimer disease. Irreversible inhibitors such as organophosphates are a separate group.
tileNotes: Edrophonium is a very short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It was historically used in the Tensilon test, in which transient improvement in strength suggested myasthenia gravis.
Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is used to reverse central and peripheral effects of anticholinergic toxicity, such as atropine poisoning.
Pyridostigmine is a quaternary amine that does not readily enter the brain. It is the standard symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis, increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.
Donepezil is a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It is used for symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer disease, aiming to boost cholinergic transmission in the brain.

NEU-016.detail: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder, usually caused by antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, that produces fatigable weakness worsening with use and improving with rest. Extraocular, eyelid and bulbar muscles are commonly involved, causing ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia and dysarthria, while pupillary function is typically preserved. Similar oculobulbar symptoms occur in botulism and Lambert-Eaton syndrome, so fatigability and pupil sparing help distinguish myasthenia.
tileNotes: Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid. In myasthenia gravis it often worsens with sustained upgaze or later in the day, reflecting fatigable levator weakness.
Diplopia is double vision from misaligned eyes. Fatigable weakness of extraocular muscles in myasthenia gravis produces variable diplopia, while the pupils are typically spared.
Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing. Bulbar muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis can make swallowing tire during a meal and raises aspiration risk.
Dysarthria is difficulty articulating speech due to weak or poorly coordinated speech muscles. In myasthenia gravis, speech may become slurred or nasal with prolonged talking.

NEU-017.detail: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, which reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Patients have proximal weakness and reduced reflexes that transiently improve after brief exercise, unlike myasthenia gravis. Roughly half of cases are paraneoplastic, most often with small cell lung carcinoma, so a new diagnosis should prompt a search for cancer.
tileNotes: P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the motor nerve terminal let calcium in to trigger acetylcholine release. Autoantibodies against them are the cause of LEMS.
Brief exercise lets calcium build up in the nerve terminal, boosting acetylcholine release. Strength and reflexes therefore transiently improve, a feature called facilitation.
Tendon reflexes are typically reduced or absent in LEMS because acetylcholine release is impaired. They may briefly return after a short muscle contraction.
Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly linked to smoking. It is the most common tumor associated with paraneoplastic LEMS, though not every patient has cancer.

NEU-018.detail: CN III supplies levator palpebrae superioris, the medial, superior and inferior recti and inferior oblique, and carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the ciliary ganglion. The parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve, so compressive lesions such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm affect them early, producing a dilated pupil and loss of accommodation. Ischemic (diabetic) palsies damage the core of the nerve and classically spare the pupil. The unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) leave the eye resting down and out.

The medial, superior and inferior recti and inferior oblique are paralyzed, so adduction, elevation and depression are impaired. Abduction (CN VI) and intorsion (CN IV) are preserved.
Parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion also supply the ciliary muscle. Their loss prevents lens accommodation, so near vision blurs in the affected eye.

NEU-020.detail: The facial nerve carries motor fibers to facial muscles and the stapedius, taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani, and parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland via the greater petrosal nerve. A lesion proximal to these branch points, at or above the geniculate region, can affect all four functions. A distal lesion near the parotid gland causes facial weakness only, so the pattern helps localize injury.

Hyperacusis is abnormal sensitivity to loud sounds. It occurs when the nerve to stapedius is affected, because the stapedius normally dampens ossicle movement.
The greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that drive tear production. It branches at the geniculate ganglion, so only proximal lesions reduce lacrimation.

NEU-023.detail: Behind the chiasm, each side of the visual pathway carries fibers from the ipsilateral temporal retina and contralateral nasal retina, representing the contralateral visual hemifield. Lesions anywhere from the optic tract to the occipital cortex therefore produce homonymous defects. The pattern depends on the site: a complete tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, a Meyer loop (temporal lobe) lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, and an occipital lesion can produce hemianopia with macular sparing. Optic nerve lesions cause monocular loss and chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia, so neither is homonymous.
tileNotes: The optic tract runs from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous.
The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus relays tract fibers to the optic radiations. A lesion produces a contralateral homonymous field defect.

Meyer loop is the inferior part of the optic radiation that sweeps through the temporal lobe, carrying fibers from the inferior retina. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

The primary visual cortex lies along the calcarine fissure of the occipital lobe. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing in posterior cerebral artery infarction.

Noise exposure and presbycusis typically affect high frequencies, Meniere disease affects low frequencies early, and vestibular schwannoma typically causes asymmetric or unilateral loss. NEU-034.detail: Ischemic stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted, and the underlying mechanism guides investigation and secondary prevention. Main mechanisms include in-situ thrombosis of a large artery, embolism from the heart or a proximal artery, occlusion of small penetrating arteries (lacunar stroke) and global systemic hypoperfusion causing watershed infarcts. These mechanisms can overlap, which etiologic schemes such as TOAST take into account.

Lacunar strokes result from occlusion of small penetrating arteries, often from hypertension-related vessel damage. They cause small deep infarcts and classic syndromes such as pure motor stroke.
Systemic hypoperfusion, as in cardiac arrest or severe hypotension, reduces flow to the whole brain. Border zones between arterial territories are most vulnerable, producing watershed infarcts.

NEU-045.detail: The hypothalamus is a small region at the base of the brain that keeps internal conditions stable by linking the nervous and endocrine systems. It integrates signals that control hunger and satiety, body temperature, daily sleep-wake timing and pituitary hormone release. NEU-053.detail: Parkinson disease motor symptoms arise from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, so most therapies aim to restore dopaminergic signaling. Strategies include replacing the precursor (levodopa with carbidopa), directly stimulating dopamine receptors, and slowing breakdown of dopamine or levodopa by blocking COMT or MAO-B. COMT inhibitors work only as levodopa adjuncts, and anticholinergics and amantadine are other, non-included classes.

COMT inhibitors such as entacapone block catechol-O-methyltransferase, which degrades levodopa peripherally. They prolong levodopa's effect and reduce wearing-off, but are used only as adjuncts to levodopa.
MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline and rasagiline block monoamine oxidase B, slowing dopamine breakdown in the brain. They can be used alone in early disease or as add-on therapy.

NEU-055.detail: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease in which misfolded prion protein induces normal protein to misfold, causing neuronal loss. It classically presents as a dementia progressing over weeks to months, accompanied by myoclonus, with spongiform (vacuolated) change in the cortex at autopsy. NEU-058.detail: Cluster headache causes attacks of severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain lasting roughly 15 to 180 minutes, accompanied by autonomic signs on the same side as the pain. Activation of the trigeminal-autonomic reflex produces tearing, nasal discharge, congestion and a partial Horner syndrome. NEU-059.detail: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, seen classically in young women with obesity, is raised intracranial pressure without a mass, hydrocephalus or other identifiable cause. Elevated pressure produces papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus and sometimes a false-localizing sixth nerve palsy, with a high lumbar puncture opening pressure but normal CSF composition. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, because venous sinus thrombosis and certain drugs can mimic every feature, and untreated papilledema can threaten vision.
tileNotes: Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure. It is the key sign in IIH and the main threat to vision, so visual fields are monitored closely.
Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic whooshing sound in the ear synchronized with the heartbeat. It is a common symptom of IIH, thought to reflect turbulent venous flow under raised pressure.

An abducens (CN VI) palsy weakens the lateral rectus, causing horizontal double vision and impaired eye abduction. In IIH it is a false-localizing sign, arising from raised pressure on the nerve's long intracranial course.

Elevated CSF opening pressure is a high pressure reading at the start of lumbar puncture. In IIH it is accompanied by normal CSF contents and normal imaging, but raised pressure alone does not establish the diagnosis.

NEU-060.detail: Typical childhood absence seizures cause brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, often many times a day, with immediate return to normal activity. The EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, which hyperventilation can provoke. Ethosuximide is first-line when absence is the only seizure type, but it does not cover generalized tonic-clonic seizures, for which valproate or lamotrigine is used instead.
tileNotes: A brief staring spell or awareness lapse lasts seconds, during which the child stops activity and does not respond, sometimes with eyelid fluttering. These episodes are often mistaken for daydreaming.

Immediate recovery means the child resumes normal activity at once, without the postictal confusion or drowsiness that follows tonic-clonic or many focal seizures. This helps distinguish absence from focal impaired-awareness seizures.

The 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave pattern is the characteristic EEG signature of typical absence seizures. It is generalized from onset and can often be triggered by hyperventilation during the recording.

PHARM-001.detail: Phase II reactions conjugate a drug or metabolite with an endogenous polar group, usually making it more water-soluble and easier to excrete in bile or urine. Glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation and methylation are canonical examples, alongside glutathione and amino acid conjugation. Conjugation increases polarity but does not always inactivate a drug, and genetic variation in some of these enzymes, such as slow acetylators, affects drug toxicity.
tileNotes: Glucuronidation attaches glucuronic acid to a substrate, catalyzed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases. It is the most common phase II pathway and is also how bilirubin is conjugated.

Acetylation transfers an acetyl group, mainly via N-acetyltransferase. Genetic slow acetylators have higher levels of drugs such as isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide, raising the risk of toxicity and drug-induced lupus.
Sulfation adds a sulfate group through sulfotransferase enzymes. It is an important phase II route for acetaminophen and some hormones and is readily saturated at high doses.

Methylation transfers a methyl group, typically from S-adenosylmethionine. Examples include catechol-O-methyltransferase acting on catecholamines and thiopurine methyltransferase acting on azathioprine and mercaptopurine.

PHARM-002.detail: CYP inducers increase the amount of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, typically over days to weeks, accelerating metabolism of substrate drugs. This can lower levels of drugs such as warfarin, oral contraceptives and some antiretrovirals, leading to therapeutic failure. Rifampin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and phenytoin are classic inducers, though the isoenzymes affected and the size of the effect vary by drug and substrate.
tileNotes: Rifampin is a rifamycin antibiotic used for tuberculosis and other infections. It is one of the most potent CYP inducers and can markedly reduce levels of many coadministered drugs, including oral contraceptives and warfarin.
Phenobarbital is a barbiturate antiseizure drug and sedative. It induces several CYP enzymes and can lower concentrations of other drugs it is combined with.
Carbamazepine is an antiseizure and mood-stabilizing drug. It induces CYP enzymes, including its own metabolism (autoinduction), so its levels fall over the first weeks of therapy.
Phenytoin is an antiseizure drug with nonlinear (saturable) kinetics. It induces hepatic CYP enzymes and can reduce the effectiveness of drugs such as oral contraceptives.

Rifampin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and phenytoin are classic inducers, though the isoenzymes affected and the size of the effect vary by drug and substrate.
tileNotes: Rifampin is a rifamycin antibiotic used for tuberculosis and other infections. It is one of the most potent CYP inducers and can markedly reduce levels of many coadministered drugs, including oral contraceptives and warfarin.
Phenobarbital is a barbiturate antiseizure drug and sedative. It induces several CYP enzymes and can lower concentrations of other drugs it is combined with.
Carbamazepine is an antiseizure and mood-stabilizing drug. It induces CYP enzymes, including its own metabolism (autoinduction), so its levels fall over the first weeks of therapy.
Phenytoin is an antiseizure drug with nonlinear (saturable) kinetics. It induces hepatic CYP enzymes and can reduce the effectiveness of drugs such as oral contraceptives.
