PHARM-003.detail: CYP inhibitors reduce the activity of one or more hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, slowing metabolism of substrate drugs and raising their levels, often within days. This can cause toxicity, such as bleeding with warfarin or arrhythmias and myopathy with other substrates. The predominant enzyme differs among these drugs: clarithromycin and ritonavir strongly inhibit CYP3A4, amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 and 2D6, and cimetidine is a weaker, broad inhibitor.
tileNotes: Cimetidine is an H2 receptor antagonist used to reduce gastric acid. It is a comparatively weak inhibitor of several CYP enzymes, which is why other H2 blockers are usually preferred when interactions matter.
Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic with a very long half-life. It inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP2D6, so it can raise warfarin levels and often requires dose reduction of interacting drugs.
Clarithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic and a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. It can increase levels of drugs such as some statins and calcium channel blockers, raising the risk of adverse effects.
Ritonavir is an HIV protease inhibitor and one of the most potent CYP3A4 inhibitors. It is now used mainly at low doses as a pharmacokinetic booster to raise levels of other antiretrovirals.

PHARM-006.detail: Direct muscarinic agonists bind and activate muscarinic acetylcholine receptors themselves, rather than increasing acetylcholine by blocking its breakdown. Their uses follow the target organs: pilocarpine and cevimeline stimulate salivary and lacrimal secretion in Sjogren syndrome, bethanechol stimulates bladder and bowel in urinary retention or GI atony, and methacholine provokes bronchoconstriction to diagnose asthma. Cevimeline is a direct muscarinic agonist with activity at M1 and M3 receptors. It is used to increase salivation and relieve dry mouth in Sjogren syndrome.

Bethanechol is a choline ester that directly stimulates muscarinic receptors and resists cholinesterase. It has little nicotinic activity and is used for nonobstructive urinary retention and GI atony.
Methacholine is a choline ester and direct muscarinic agonist. It is inhaled in bronchoprovocation testing, where an exaggerated bronchoconstrictive response supports a diagnosis of asthma.

PHARM-008.detail: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. The peripheral muscarinic excess produces miosis, lacrimation, bronchospasm with bronchorrhea, and diarrhea, often summarized as DUMBELS or SLUDGE features. Atropine reverses these muscarinic effects, while nicotinic weakness and central seizures are separate parts of the toxidrome; direct muscarinic agonist excess reproduces the same findings.
tileNotes: Miosis is constriction of the pupil caused by contraction of the iris sphincter muscle. Muscarinic stimulation produces pinpoint pupils in organophosphate poisoning, though opioid toxicity can also cause them.
Lacrimation is excess tear production driven by muscarinic stimulation of lacrimal glands. It reflects the widespread increase in glandular secretions in cholinergic toxicity.

Bronchospasm is constriction of airway smooth muscle via M3 receptors, often accompanied by profuse bronchial secretions. Together these are a major cause of respiratory failure in organophosphate poisoning and the key target for atropine.
Diarrhea results from muscarinic stimulation of gut motility and secretion. It is part of the classic gastrointestinal picture of cholinergic excess, along with cramping and vomiting.

PHARM-009.detail: Antimuscarinic toxicity, from drugs such as atropine, tricyclic antidepressants and first-generation antihistamines, blocks parasympathetic and sweat gland muscarinic receptors. The result is dilated pupils, hot dry skin, urinary retention and tachycardia, often with delirium. Dry skin is the key bedside clue separating it from sympathomimetic toxicity, which also causes mydriasis and tachycardia but with sweating.
tileNotes: Mydriasis is pupillary dilation. Blocking muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter leaves the dilator unopposed, and the pupils also respond poorly to light, contributing to blurred vision.

Dry skin results from blockade of sympathetic cholinergic (muscarinic) receptors on sweat glands. Anhidrosis is the classic clue that distinguishes anticholinergic from sympathomimetic toxicity, which causes sweating.
Urinary retention is inability to empty the bladder. Muscarinic blockade relaxes the detrusor muscle, impairing voiding, especially in older men with prostatic enlargement.
Tachycardia is an elevated heart rate. Blocking vagal (muscarinic M2) input to the sinoatrial node removes parasympathetic slowing, so heart rate rises.

PHARM-010.detail: Central alpha-2 agonists stimulate presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem and elsewhere, reducing sympathetic outflow and altering central neurotransmission. Shared effects include lowered blood pressure, sedation and dry mouth, yet their clinical uses differ: clonidine for hypertension and withdrawal symptoms, guanfacine for ADHD, dexmedetomidine for ICU sedation, and tizanidine for spasticity. Abrupt stopping of clonidine can cause rebound hypertension.
tileNotes: Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the brainstem. It is used for hypertension, ADHD and opioid withdrawal symptoms, and sudden discontinuation can cause rebound hypertension.
Guanfacine is a central alpha-2 agonist, more selective for the alpha-2A subtype than clonidine. It is used mainly as a nonstimulant treatment for ADHD and less often for hypertension.

Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha-2 agonist given intravenously. It provides sedation with relatively little respiratory depression, making it useful in intensive care and procedural settings.

Tizanidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces spinal motor neuron excitability. It is used to treat spasticity, for example in multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury, and can cause hypotension and sedation.

PHARM-011.detail: Alpha-1 antagonists block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle and in the prostate and bladder neck. Prazosin, terazosin and doxazosin have prominent vascular effects, lowering blood pressure and causing first-dose orthostatic hypotension, while tamsulosin is relatively selective for the alpha-1A subtype in the urinary tract. They share a receptor mechanism, but their main clinical uses differ.

Terazosin is a longer-acting alpha-1 antagonist that relaxes both vascular and prostatic smooth muscle. It is used for hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, with a risk of orthostatic hypotension.

Doxazosin is a long-acting alpha-1 antagonist used for hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Like the other nonselective agents, it can cause dizziness and orthostatic hypotension, especially after the first dose.

Tamsulosin is an alpha-1 antagonist relatively selective for the alpha-1A subtype found in the prostate. It relieves urinary symptoms of BPH with less effect on blood pressure, and it is linked to floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery.

PHARM-013.detail: Nonselective beta blockers antagonize both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, unlike cardioselective agents such as metoprolol, and these four lack the added alpha-1 blockade of carvedilol and labetalol. Beta-2 blockade explains why they can provoke bronchospasm in asthma and why propranolol and nadolol help prevent variceal bleeding. Sotalol also blocks potassium channels (class III action), which adds to rather than replaces its beta blockade.
tileNotes: Nadolol is a long-acting, water-soluble nonselective beta blocker. It is used for hypertension, angina and prevention of variceal bleeding in portal hypertension.

Propranolol is a lipophilic nonselective beta blocker that enters the CNS. Its uses include essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, performance anxiety, thyrotoxicosis symptoms and variceal bleeding prophylaxis.
Timolol is a nonselective beta blocker most often used as eye drops for glaucoma, where it reduces aqueous humor production. Systemic absorption can still cause bradycardia or bronchospasm.
Sotalol is a nonselective beta blocker that also blocks potassium channels, giving it class III antiarrhythmic activity. It prolongs the QT interval and carries a risk of torsades de pointes.

PHARM-017.detail: Each of these sympathomimetics activates cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing myocardial contractility. Their overall hemodynamic effects differ because of varying alpha-1 and beta-2 activity: dobutamine is mainly an inotrope, isoproterenol strongly increases heart rate and causes vasodilation, and epinephrine and norepinephrine add vasoconstriction. Norepinephrine can even cause reflex bradycardia as blood pressure rises, despite its direct beta-1 effect.
tileNotes: Dobutamine is a synthetic catecholamine acting mainly on beta-1 receptors. It increases contractility and cardiac output, making it useful in cardiogenic shock and cardiac stress testing.

Isoproterenol is a nonselective beta agonist with little alpha activity. Beta-1 effects increase heart rate and contractility, while beta-2 vasodilation can lower diastolic pressure; it is sometimes used for bradycardia.
Epinephrine stimulates alpha and beta receptors, increasing contractility and heart rate through beta-1. It is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and is used in cardiac arrest.

Norepinephrine acts mainly on alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors, causing vasoconstriction with some inotropy. It is a first-line vasopressor in septic shock, and the rise in blood pressure can trigger reflex bradycardia.

PHARM-019.detail: Chelating agents bind metal ions to form stable complexes that are excreted in urine or stool. Lead, mercury, arsenic and iron toxicity can all be treated this way, but the agent depends on the metal, its chemical form and the acuity: dimercaprol, succimer (DMSA) or EDTA for lead, DMSA or DMPS for mercury and arsenic, and deferoxamine or deferasirox for iron. This is a treatment grouping, and the list is not exhaustive.
tileNotes: Lead poisoning can cause microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal pain, neuropathy and cognitive problems in children. Depending on severity, chelation uses succimer, EDTA or dimercaprol.

Mercury toxicity varies with form: elemental vapor affects lungs and nervous system, while inorganic salts injure the gut and kidneys. Chelators such as DMSA or DMPS are used for appropriate exposures.
Arsenic poisoning can cause vomiting, rice-water diarrhea, garlic breath, QT prolongation and later peripheral neuropathy. Chelation with dimercaprol, DMSA or DMPS is used depending on the setting.

Iron overdose, often accidental ingestion of supplements by children, causes GI injury, metabolic acidosis and hepatotoxicity. Deferoxamine treats acute toxicity, and deferasirox is used for chronic iron overload.

PLEXUS-GEN-001.detail: Nucleosomes, the basic units of chromatin, consist of DNA wrapped around a protein core called the histone octamer. This octamer contains two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. H1 is a linker histone that binds DNA between nucleosomes and is not part of the core, and modifications of histone tails such as acetylation and methylation regulate gene expression.
tileNotes: H2A is a core histone that pairs with H2B to form dimers within the octamer. Variants of H2A help regulate processes such as DNA repair and transcription.
H2B is a core histone that forms a dimer with H2A. Two H2A-H2B dimers sit on either side of the central H3-H4 tetramer in the nucleosome.
H3 is a core histone that pairs with H4 to form the central tetramer of the octamer. Its tail is a frequent site of acetylation and methylation that influence gene expression.
H4 is a core histone and partner of H3 in the central tetramer. It is among the most highly conserved proteins, and acetylation of its tail is associated with open, active chromatin.

PLEXUS-GEN-002.detail: Topoisomerase inhibitors trap the enzyme on DNA after it has cut the strand, so breaks accumulate and the cell dies. The camptothecins (irinotecan, topotecan) act on topoisomerase I, which makes single-strand breaks. Etoposide (an epipodophyllotoxin) and the anthracyclines such as doxorubicin act on topoisomerase II, which makes double-strand breaks. Doxorubicin is often remembered only as a DNA intercalator and free-radical generator, but topoisomerase II inhibition is a core part of its mechanism. Do not confuse this group with microtubule inhibitors (vincristine, paclitaxel) or alkylating agents.
tileNotes: A camptothecin derivative that inhibits topoisomerase I; used in colorectal cancer and known for causing severe diarrhea.
A camptothecin derivative that inhibits topoisomerase I; used in small cell lung and ovarian cancer.
An epipodophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II, acting in late S and G2 phase; used in testicular and small cell lung cancer.
An anthracycline that intercalates into DNA, generates free radicals, and inhibits topoisomerase II; its signature toxicity is dilated cardiomyopathy.

history.detail: Topoisomerases relieve DNA supercoiling during replication and transcription by cutting and resealing DNA strands. These anticancer drugs trap the enzyme-DNA complex, producing DNA breaks that kill dividing cells. Irinotecan and topotecan, camptothecin derivatives, inhibit topoisomerase I, which cuts one strand, while the epipodophyllotoxins etoposide and teniposide inhibit topoisomerase II, which cuts both strands.
tileNotes: Irinotecan is a camptothecin-derived topoisomerase I inhibitor used mainly in colorectal cancer. Severe diarrhea and myelosuppression are characteristic adverse effects.
Topotecan is a camptothecin derivative that inhibits topoisomerase I. It is used for cancers such as small cell lung cancer and ovarian cancer, with myelosuppression as its main toxicity.
Etoposide is an epipodophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II, causing double-strand DNA breaks. It acts mainly in the late S and G2 phases and is used for testicular and small cell lung cancers.
Teniposide is an epipodophyllotoxin closely related to etoposide. It inhibits topoisomerase II and has been used mainly in some childhood leukemias.

PLEXUS-GEN-004.detail: Trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders arise when a run of three nucleotides becomes abnormally long and unstable, and it can expand further between generations. PLEXUS-GEN-013.detail: The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a specific DNA segment through repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension. Its core reagents are a DNA template, a pair of primers flanking the target, a thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq, and dNTPs, with buffer and magnesium ions also required. The primers set which segment is copied, and the heat-stable polymerase survives the repeated high-temperature denaturation steps.
tileNotes: The DNA template is the sample containing the target sequence to be copied. It is separated into single strands during the high-temperature denaturation step of each cycle.

The two flanking primers are short single-stranded oligonucleotides complementary to sequences on either side of the target. They define the region that is amplified and provide a starting point for the polymerase.
Taq polymerase is a heat-stable DNA polymerase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus. It survives repeated denaturation cycles and extends primers to synthesize new DNA strands.
Deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs: dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP) are the building blocks of DNA. The polymerase incorporates them into each newly synthesized strand.

PLEXUS-GEN-021.detail: Beyond acute vaso-occlusion, sickle cell disease has several classic complications. Parvovirus B19 can halt red cell production and cause a transient aplastic crisis, repeated splenic infarction leads to functional asplenia, osteomyelitis is characteristically caused by Salmonella (though Staphylococcus aureus is also common), and the hypoxic renal medulla is prone to papillary necrosis. Renal papillary necrosis is death of the renal papillae, which lie in the low-oxygen, hypertonic medulla that promotes sickling. It can cause hematuria and may also be seen in sickle cell trait.

PLEXUS-GEN-030.detail: Trisomy 21 is associated with several structural congenital anomalies that affect the gut, heart and cervical spine. Atrioventricular septal defect is the characteristic cardiac lesion, and duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease are classic gastrointestinal associations. PLX-BCH-001.detail: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active form of vitamin B1, is the shared cofactor for these four enzymes. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase are multienzyme complexes that also need lipoate, FAD, NAD+ and CoA, whereas transketolase needs only TPP. Thiamine deficiency therefore impairs glucose oxidation, which is why glucose given before thiamine can worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.

All four are lost in the urine, but only cystine is poorly soluble, so it precipitates as hexagonal crystals and forms recurrent kidney stones. PLX-BCH-004.detail: Pyruvate sits at a metabolic crossroads, and its fate depends on cellular energy state and oxygen availability. Pyruvate dehydrogenase makes acetyl-CoA irreversibly, pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis or TCA replenishment, lactate dehydrogenase makes lactate to regenerate NAD+, and alanine aminotransferase makes alanine to carry nitrogen. Each enzyme has its own cofactor: TPP and others for PDH, biotin for pyruvate carboxylase, NADH for LDH and B6 for ALT.

Lactate is produced from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Red blood cells and hypoxic tissues rely on this route.
Alanine is formed when alanine aminotransferase (ALT) transfers an amino group to pyruvate, a B6-dependent reaction. In the Cahill cycle alanine carries nitrogen from muscle to the liver.

Recognizing the enzyme and cofactor for each step is a staple exam question.
tileNotes: Acetyl-CoA is the two-carbon unit that enters the TCA cycle or fatty acid synthesis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase forms it from pyruvate in an irreversible reaction.
Oxaloacetate is a four-carbon TCA cycle intermediate and the first committed substrate of gluconeogenesis. Pyruvate carboxylase, a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme, forms it from pyruvate.
Lactate is produced from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Red blood cells and hypoxic tissues rely on this route.
Alanine is formed when alanine aminotransferase (ALT) transfers an amino group to pyruvate, a B6-dependent reaction. In the Cahill cycle alanine carries nitrogen from muscle to the liver.

PLX-BCH-005.detail: Gluconeogenesis reuses most glycolytic enzymes but must bypass three irreversible steps: pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and hexokinase/glucokinase. Pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase together bypass pyruvate kinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses PFK-1, and glucose-6-phosphatase bypasses hexokinase. Glucose-6-phosphatase is found mainly in liver and kidney, which is why muscle cannot release free glucose into the blood.
tileNotes: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in mitochondria, using biotin and ATP. Acetyl-CoA activates it, and it is the first step in bypassing pyruvate kinase.
PEP carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, using GTP. Together with pyruvate carboxylase it completes the bypass of pyruvate kinase.

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase removes a phosphate from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to form fructose-6-phosphate, bypassing PFK-1. It is a major regulated step, inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and AMP.
Glucose-6-phosphatase, in the endoplasmic reticulum of liver and kidney cells, releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate. Its deficiency causes von Gierke disease (GSD type I).

PLX-BCH-006.detail: Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase normally converts it onward to fructose. Tissues with low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase trap sorbitol during hyperglycemia, drawing in water and causing osmotic injury. This pathway is one contributor, alongside other mechanisms, to diabetic cataracts, retinopathy, nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy.
tileNotes: The lens is the transparent structure that focuses light onto the retina. Sorbitol accumulation in lens cells causes osmotic swelling and contributes to diabetic cataracts.
The retina is the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye. Sorbitol trapping in retinal cells is one proposed contributor to diabetic retinopathy.

The kidneys have low sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, so sorbitol made by aldose reductase builds up during sustained hyperglycemia. This osmotic stress is one of several factors in diabetic nephropathy.
Schwann cells form myelin around peripheral nerve axons. Sorbitol buildup in these cells is thought to contribute to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

PLX-BCH-010.detail: Microtubules are dynamic polymers of tubulin needed for intracellular transport, cell shape and the mitotic spindle. These four drugs all interfere with microtubule function, but their targets and uses differ: mebendazole acts on helminths, griseofulvin on dermatophytes, colchicine on neutrophils in gout, and vincristine on dividing cancer cells. Their mechanisms are not identical, and not all of them are anticancer agents.
tileNotes: Mebendazole is a benzimidazole anthelmintic used for intestinal worms such as pinworm. It binds parasite tubulin and impairs microtubule-dependent glucose uptake by the worm.
Griseofulvin is an oral antifungal for dermatophyte infections of skin, hair and nails. It disrupts fungal microtubule function and so interferes with mitosis.
Colchicine is used for acute gout and familial Mediterranean fever. It binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule polymerization, reducing neutrophil migration and degranulation.
Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid chemotherapy drug that binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, arresting cells in mitosis. Peripheral neuropathy is its classic dose-limiting toxicity.

PLX-BCH-011.detail: Copper deficiency, as in Menkes disease, impairs all of these enzymes, which explains its combination of neurologic decline, hypopigmentation, connective tissue fragility and oxidative injury. Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc isoform; mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 uses manganese instead and would not fit. Zinc-dependent enzymes such as carbonic anhydrase are a common look-alike group.

Tyrosinase converts tyrosine toward melanin. Copper is its catalytic metal, so copper deficiency causes hypopigmentation.
Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and elastin. It is copper-dependent, and its loss in Menkes disease weakens connective tissue and vessels.
Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc enzyme that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Copper is its catalytic metal.

PLX-BCH-012.detail: NADPH, generated mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway, supplies reducing power for biosynthesis and redox reactions. These four enzymes consume it to regenerate reduced glutathione, synthesize cholesterol, build fatty acids and produce the superoxide of the phagocyte respiratory burst. Clinically, G6PD deficiency limits NADPH and causes oxidative hemolysis, while defective NADPH oxidase causes chronic granulomatous disease.
tileNotes: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to convert oxidized glutathione back to its reduced form. This keeps red cells protected from oxidative damage, which fails in G6PD deficiency.
HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and uses NADPH as its reductant. It is the target of statin drugs.
Fatty acid synthase builds palmitate from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA in the cytosol. Each elongation cycle uses NADPH for its reduction steps.

NADPH oxidase in phagocytes uses NADPH to generate superoxide during the respiratory burst. It produces reactive oxygen species rather than removing them, and its deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease.

PLX-BCH-013.detail: Homocysteine is cleared either by remethylation to methionine, which needs B12 and the folate derivative made via MTHFR, or by transsulfuration to cystathionine via the B6-dependent enzyme cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). A defect in either route raises homocysteine. Methylmalonic acid and methionine levels help sort the causes: MMA is high in B12 deficiency but not folate deficiency, and methionine is high in CBS deficiency.

Vitamin B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase, which remethylates homocysteine. Deficiency raises both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.
Cystathionine beta-synthase uses B6 to convert homocysteine and serine to cystathionine. Its deficiency causes classic homocystinuria, with high homocysteine and high methionine.
MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase) produces the methyl-tetrahydrofolate used for homocysteine remethylation. Severe deficiency raises homocysteine with low or normal methionine.

PLX-BCH-014.detail: These are recognized inherited urea cycle disorders, and each impairs conversion of ammonia to urea, causing hyperammonemia. OTC deficiency is X-linked and the most common; the others are autosomal recessive. NAGS deficiency acts by failing to make N-acetylglutamate, the required activator of CPS I, and arginase deficiency typically presents as progressive spastic diplegia with less prominent neonatal hyperammonemia, so presentations are not uniform.
tileNotes: Ornithine transcarbamylase combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine in the mitochondria. Its X-linked deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and characteristically raises urinary orotic acid.

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate as the first urea cycle step. Its deficiency causes hyperammonemia without the orotic aciduria seen in OTC deficiency.

Arginase cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine as the final urea cycle step. Its deficiency classically causes progressive spastic diplegia and high arginine, with less prominent neonatal hyperammonemia.
N-acetylglutamate synthase makes N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory allosteric activator of CPS I. Its deficiency reduces CPS I activity rather than removing a core cycle enzyme.

PLX-BCH-016.detail: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, is the cofactor for the amino acid decarboxylases that form these neurotransmitters. GABA comes from glutamate, histamine from histidine, dopamine from L-DOPA and serotonin from 5-hydroxytryptophan. Serotonin and dopamine synthesis each require a hydroxylation step before decarboxylation, and B6 deficiency, as with isoniazid use, can cause seizures partly through reduced GABA.
tileNotes: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, formed from glutamate by the PLP-dependent enzyme glutamate decarboxylase. Reduced GABA synthesis helps explain seizures in B6 deficiency.
Histamine is formed by PLP-dependent decarboxylation of histidine. It acts in allergic responses, gastric acid secretion and as a neurotransmitter promoting wakefulness.
Dopamine is a catecholamine formed when aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, a PLP enzyme, decarboxylates L-DOPA. L-DOPA itself comes from tyrosine hydroxylation.
Serotonin (5-HT) is made from tryptophan in two steps: hydroxylation to 5-hydroxytryptophan, then PLP-dependent decarboxylation. It is not a one-step conversion from tryptophan.

PLX-BCH-017.detail: Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, which stabilize collagen. Without it, collagen is weak, so small vessels, gums, hair follicles and healing wounds are affected. Corkscrew hairs with perifollicular hemorrhage are especially suggestive, although each finding alone can have other causes. Scurvy is seen in people with very restricted diets, such as those with alcohol use disorder or food insecurity.
tileNotes: Corkscrew hairs are coiled, fragmented body hairs caused by defective keratin and follicle structure in vitamin C deficiency. They are a highly suggestive sign of scurvy.
Perifollicular hemorrhages are small bleeds around hair follicles, often on the legs. They reflect fragile capillaries from defective collagen and frequently accompany corkscrew hairs.
Gingival bleeding refers to swollen, bleeding gums. In scurvy weak collagen in gum tissue causes this classic oral finding, though gum bleeding has many other causes.
Wound healing depends on new, cross-linked collagen. Impaired collagen hydroxylation in vitamin C deficiency leads to poor healing and breakdown of old scars.

PLX-BCH-018.detail: Osteogenesis imperfecta is usually caused by mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 that reduce or impair type I collagen. Because type I collagen is abundant in bone, sclera, dentin and the ear ossicles, the disease causes fragile bones, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta and hearing loss. Severity varies widely by type, and hearing loss in particular is age and subtype dependent, so not every patient has all four.
tileNotes: Minimal-trauma fractures occur with little or no injury because bone is fragile. In osteogenesis imperfecta they are the defining feature and can be mistaken for child abuse.
Blue sclerae occur when thin, collagen-deficient sclera lets the underlying choroid show through. They are a classic, though not universal, sign of osteogenesis imperfecta.
Opalescent teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta) are discolored, translucent and wear easily because dentin contains defective type I collagen. They are a recognized feature in many patients.
Hearing loss in osteogenesis imperfecta stems from abnormal ossicles and inner ear structures. It typically develops progressively from early adulthood and varies by subtype.

PLX-BCH-019.detail: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase in heme synthesis. Attacks, often triggered by certain drugs, alcohol, fasting or hormonal changes, cause accumulation of ALA and porphobilinogen, producing abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms and urine that may darken on standing. Unlike porphyria cutanea tarda, AIP does not cause photosensitivity, and treatment includes hemin and glucose.
tileNotes: Severe, often poorly localized abdominal pain is the most common symptom of an AIP attack. It is neurovisceral in origin, so the abdominal exam may be surprisingly unremarkable.
Polyneuropathy in AIP is mainly a motor neuropathy that can progress to weakness and, in severe attacks, respiratory compromise. It reflects neurotoxicity during attacks.
Psychiatric disturbances such as anxiety, confusion, hallucinations or psychosis can occur during AIP attacks. They may lead to misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric illness.
Urine in AIP may be normal when passed but darken to a reddish or port-wine color on standing as porphobilinogen converts to porphyrins. The color change is variable and not always present.

PLX-BCH-020.detail: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria and results from reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity. Iron overload, alcohol use, hepatitis C and smoking are associated susceptibility factors that make symptomatic disease more likely, but none is sufficient alone. Skin lesions themselves arise when accumulated porphyrins react with sunlight, causing blistering and fragility on sun-exposed skin, so these factors should be distinguished from the UV trigger.
tileNotes: Iron overload, including from hemochromatosis gene variants, promotes inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in the liver. Reducing iron by phlebotomy is a standard treatment for PCT.
Alcohol use is a well-recognized susceptibility factor for porphyria cutanea tarda. It is thought to act partly through increased hepatic iron and oxidative stress.
Hepatitis C infection is strongly associated with porphyria cutanea tarda. Patients presenting with PCT are commonly screened for HCV.
Smoking is another recognized susceptibility factor for symptomatic PCT. Like the other factors, it increases risk but does not cause the disease on its own.

PLX-BCH-021.detail: Intermediate filaments are cytoskeletal proteins whose type reflects a cell's lineage, which makes them useful immunohistochemical markers. Cytokeratin marks epithelial cells, vimentin mesenchymal cells, desmin muscle and GFAP glial cells. Pathologists use panels of these stains to help classify poorly differentiated tumors, but no single stain is diagnostic on its own.
tileNotes: Cytokeratins are intermediate filaments of epithelial cells. Positive staining supports an epithelial origin, such as a carcinoma.
Vimentin is the intermediate filament of mesenchymal cells such as fibroblasts and endothelium. It is commonly expressed in sarcomas but also appears in some other tumors.
Desmin is the intermediate filament of smooth, skeletal and cardiac muscle. Staining suggests muscle differentiation, as in leiomyosarcoma or rhabdomyosarcoma.
GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is found in astrocytes and other glial cells. It supports a glial origin, as in astrocytomas.

PLX-BCH-022.detail: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive and often involves dynein arm defects. Poor clearance causes chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent or chronic otitis media from childhood, and immotile sperm cause male infertility. Cystic fibrosis shares bronchiectasis, sinusitis and male infertility, but CF infertility comes from absent vas deferens rather than immotile sperm, and chronic otitis media is far more typical of PCD. Situs inversus occurs in about half of patients (Kartagener syndrome).
tileNotes: Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation from repeated infection when cilia cannot clear mucus.
Recurrent sinusitis reflects failed ciliary clearance of the paranasal sinuses and is nearly universal in PCD.
Chronic otitis media results from poor ciliary clearance of the middle ear and eustachian tube and is a typical childhood feature of PCD.
Male infertility occurs because sperm flagella share the defective axoneme and are immotile.

history.detail: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually an autosomal recessive defect in motile cilia, often involving dynein arms. Poor mucociliary clearance leads to chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis, immotile sperm cause male infertility, and dysfunctional embryonic nodal cilia randomize organ laterality. Situs inversus occurs in only about half of patients and infertility is not universal; the subset with situs inversus is called Kartagener syndrome.
tileNotes: Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of the bronchi from chronic infection and inflammation. In primary ciliary dyskinesia it develops because cilia cannot clear mucus from the airways.
Recurrent sinusitis results from impaired mucociliary clearance in the paranasal sinuses. Chronic upper airway symptoms often begin in early childhood in this disorder.
Situs inversus is a mirror-image reversal of the thoracic and abdominal organs. It arises when nodal cilia fail to establish normal left-right asymmetry, and occurs in about half of patients.
Male infertility in primary ciliary dyskinesia stems from immotile or poorly motile sperm, whose flagella share the ciliary structure. It is common but not universal.

PLX-BCH-023.detail: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis type II) is an autosomal recessive defect of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase in the Golgi, so lysosomal enzymes are not tagged with mannose-6-phosphate. PLX-BCH-041.detail: Von Gierke disease (GSD type I) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The liver cannot release free glucose, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, while trapped glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into lactate, triglyceride and uric acid production. Cori disease, by contrast, has milder hypoglycemia with normal lactate and uric acid.

PLX-BCH-043.detail: McArdle disease (GSD type V) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase), so muscle cannot break down its own glycogen during exertion. PLX-BCH-044.detail: Ketone bodies made in the liver during fasting or carbohydrate restriction are exported and oxidized by tissues with mitochondria and the enzyme succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase). The liver lacks thiophorase and red blood cells lack mitochondria, so neither can oxidize ketones.

PLX-BCH-047.detail: The pancreas secretes its proteases as inactive zymogens so they cannot digest the gland itself. In the duodenum, brush-border enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidases A and B. Trypsin therefore sits at the center of protein digestion, and premature intrapancreatic activation of these enzymes is a key concept in acute pancreatitis.
tileNotes: Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive precursor of chymotrypsin, an endopeptidase that cleaves peptide bonds next to aromatic amino acids. Trypsin cleavage in the duodenal lumen converts it to its active form.
Proelastase is the zymogen form of elastase, a pancreatic endopeptidase that can digest elastin and other proteins. Like the other pancreatic protease precursors, it is switched on by trypsin.

Procarboxypeptidase A is the precursor of carboxypeptidase A, a zinc-containing exopeptidase that removes C-terminal amino acids, favoring aromatic and bulky hydrophobic residues. It becomes active only after trypsin cleaves it.

A distinct enzyme from the A form, procarboxypeptidase B gives rise to carboxypeptidase B, which removes C-terminal basic residues such as lysine and arginine. Trypsin is also responsible for its activation.

PLX-BCH-048.detail: Tyrosine, made from phenylalanine by phenylalanine hydroxylase or obtained from the diet, is the starting point for several important products. Through a series of enzymatic steps it gives rise to the catecholamines dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine, and in melanocytes tyrosinase converts it toward the pigment melanin. These pathways explain links between disorders such as phenylketonuria and albinism and findings like reduced pigmentation.

Produced mainly in the adrenal medulla, epinephrine is made from norepinephrine by the enzyme PNMT, whose expression is enhanced by cortisol. It is the final catecholamine in the tyrosine pathway.
Melanin is the pigment of skin, hair and eyes, synthesized in melanocytes beginning with tyrosinase acting on tyrosine. Tyrosinase defects cause albinism, showing the tyrosine origin of this pigment.

PLX-BCH-071.detail: Protein structure is described in four hierarchical levels. The amino acid sequence (primary) determines local folding patterns (secondary), the overall three-dimensional shape of a single chain (tertiary) and, for proteins with more than one chain, how subunits assemble (quaternary). Small changes at one level can alter function, as when a single amino acid substitution in beta-globin causes sickle cell disease.
tileNotes: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. It is encoded by the gene and ultimately determines all higher levels of folding.
Secondary structure describes local folding patterns such as alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets. These are stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.
Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide chain. It is held together by side-chain interactions such as hydrophobic contacts, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges.

Quaternary structure describes how separate polypeptide subunits associate in a multimeric protein. Hemoglobin, with two alpha and two beta chains, is the classic example; single-chain proteins lack this level.

PLX-BCH-072.detail: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, is a cofactor for many enzymes, though it participates through different mechanisms. It is required for amino group transfer by ALT and AST, for the first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis by ALA synthase, and for glycogen breakdown by glycogen phosphorylase. This explains why B6 deficiency can affect amino acid metabolism and cause sideroblastic anemia.
tileNotes: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) transfers an amino group between alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate, forming pyruvate and glutamate. It uses PLP and is a sensitive serum marker of liver injury.
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) interconverts aspartate and oxaloacetate by amino group transfer, using PLP. It is found in liver, heart and muscle.
ALA synthase condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA to form aminolevulinic acid, the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis. It requires PLP, which links B6 deficiency to sideroblastic anemia.
Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen. PLP is bound to the enzyme and is required for its activity, through a mechanism distinct from transamination.

PLX-BCH-073.detail: Lipolysis, the breakdown of stored triglyceride into fatty acids and glycerol, is stimulated by catecholamines and by natriuretic peptides. Epinephrine and norepinephrine act through beta-adrenergic receptors, cAMP and protein kinase A, whereas ANP and BNP act through natriuretic peptide receptor A, cGMP and protein kinase G. Both pathways converge on lipases in adipocytes, while insulin opposes lipolysis.
tileNotes: Epinephrine is an adrenal medullary hormone released during stress and exercise. Through beta-adrenergic receptors and cAMP, it activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes.
Norepinephrine is released by sympathetic nerves that supply adipose tissue. It stimulates lipolysis through beta-adrenergic receptors and cAMP signaling.

ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) is released by atrial myocytes in response to stretch and promotes sodium excretion and vasodilation. In adipose tissue it stimulates lipolysis through cGMP signaling.
BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) is released mainly by ventricular myocytes under stretch and is used as a heart-failure marker. Like ANP, it can promote adipocyte lipolysis via a cGMP pathway.

PLX-BCH-075.detail: Ketone bodies are made in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA when fatty acid oxidation is high, as in fasting or diabetic ketoacidosis. Thiolase joins two acetyl-CoA, mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase adds a third to form HMG-CoA, HMG-CoA lyase releases acetoacetate, and beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase interconverts acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is distinct from the cytosolic isoform used in cholesterol synthesis.
tileNotes: Thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA molecules into acetoacetyl-CoA, the first step of ketogenesis. It also acts in ketone body utilization in peripheral tissues.

Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase adds acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA and is the key regulated step of ketogenesis. A separate cytosolic isoform supplies HMG-CoA for cholesterol synthesis.
HMG-CoA lyase cleaves HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. Its inherited deficiency impairs ketone production and causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase interconverts acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, using NADH in the liver and NAD+ in tissues that oxidize ketones. It participates in both ketone formation and ketone use.

PLX-BCH-076.detail: Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect in the transporter for neutral amino acids in the renal proximal tubule and intestine. Neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, are lost in urine and poorly absorbed, reducing tryptophan available for niacin synthesis. Some patients develop a pellagra-like photosensitive rash and intermittent cerebellar ataxia, especially with poor nutrition, and many remain asymptomatic. Neutral aminoaciduria distinguishes it from primary niacin deficiency.
tileNotes: Neutral aminoaciduria is excess urinary loss of neutral amino acids such as tryptophan. It reflects the renal transport defect and is the laboratory hallmark of Hartnup disease.
Reduced tryptophan availability results from both intestinal malabsorption and urinary loss. Because tryptophan is a niacin precursor, this can lead to niacin deficiency.
Pellagra-like dermatitis is a photosensitive, scaly rash on sun-exposed skin resembling that of niacin deficiency. It appears in some patients with Hartnup disease.
Cerebellar ataxia is unsteady, poorly coordinated movement caused by cerebellar dysfunction. In Hartnup disease it tends to be intermittent and linked to nutritional stress.

PLX-BCH-077.detail: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), a vitamin B6-dependent enzyme, converts L-DOPA to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. In inherited AADC deficiency, both neurotransmitters are deficient, producing oculogyric crises, hypotonia, autonomic dysfunction and developmental delay from infancy. Oculogyric crisis is the most suggestive feature, but other neurotransmitter synthesis disorders can look similar, so diagnosis relies on CSF neurotransmitter metabolites and enzyme or genetic testing.
tileNotes: Oculogyric crises are episodes of sustained, involuntary upward deviation of the eyes. They reflect dopamine deficiency and are the strongest clinical clue to AADC deficiency.
Hypotonia is reduced muscle tone, often described as a floppy infant. It is a common early sign of AADC deficiency.
Autonomic dysfunction includes problems such as excessive sweating, nasal congestion, ptosis and temperature instability. It reflects deficient catecholamine signaling.
Developmental delay means slower-than-expected achievement of motor, language or social milestones. It is a typical, often severe, feature of AADC deficiency.

PLX-BCH-078.detail: Ornithine transcarbamylase combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline in the urea cycle. In OTC deficiency, the most common urea cycle disorder and X-linked, urea production falls and ammonia accumulates, while excess carbamoyl phosphate enters pyrimidine synthesis and raises orotic acid. Elevated orotic acid separates it from CPS I deficiency, and laboratory values vary with treatment and metabolic state.
tileNotes: Hyperammonemia is a high blood ammonia level that can cause vomiting, lethargy, cerebral edema and coma. It results from impaired ammonia disposal through the urea cycle.
Elevated orotic acid arises when unused carbamoyl phosphate is diverted into pyrimidine synthesis. It distinguishes OTC deficiency from CPS I deficiency.
Low citrulline reflects the blocked step, since OTC is the enzyme that forms citrulline. Plasma amino acid analysis helps localize the urea cycle defect.
Low BUN (blood urea nitrogen) reflects reduced urea formation. In a patient with hyperammonemia, a low BUN points toward a urea cycle disorder.

PLX-BCH-079.detail: Recombinant enzymes are taken up by cells through mannose or mannose-6-phosphate receptors and delivered to lysosomes. Approved therapies include agalsidase for Fabry disease, imiglucerase for Gaucher disease, laronidase for Hurler syndrome and alglucosidase alfa for Pompe disease. Enzyme replacement does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so it treats visceral and muscle disease better than neurologic disease. Hunter syndrome and acid sphingomyelinase deficiency also have approved enzyme replacement.
tileNotes: Fabry disease is X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, treated with recombinant alpha-galactosidase A.
Gaucher disease is glucocerebrosidase deficiency, treated with recombinant glucocerebrosidase such as imiglucerase.
Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, treated with laronidase, often with stem cell transplant.
Pompe disease (GSD II) is lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, treated with recombinant acid alpha-glucosidase.

history.detail: Lysosomal storage diseases result from deficient lysosomal enzymes that allow undegraded substrates to accumulate in cells. For Fabry, Gaucher, Hurler and Pompe disease, intravenous recombinant enzyme replacement therapy is a described management approach. It is not curative, and eligibility and benefit differ; infused enzymes cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so central nervous system disease responds less well.
tileNotes: Fabry disease is an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A with accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. It causes painful neuropathy, angiokeratomas, reduced sweating and renal and cardiac disease.
Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase, with lipid-laden macrophages resembling crumpled tissue paper. It causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias and bone disease.

Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase with accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate. Features include coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly and developmental delay.
Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) is deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase. The infantile form causes cardiomegaly and profound hypotonia.

PLX-HEM-001.detail: Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor and ticlopidine block the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, reducing platelet activation and aggregation. Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticlopidine are thienopyridine prodrugs that bind irreversibly, whereas ticagrelor is a direct-acting, reversible antagonist. These drugs are used with aspirin after acute coronary syndromes and coronary stenting, and their differences in activation, reversibility and adverse effects are frequently tested.
tileNotes: Clopidogrel is a thienopyridine prodrug activated by hepatic CYP2C19, then irreversibly blocks P2Y12. Patients with reduced CYP2C19 function may get less antiplatelet effect.

Prasugrel is a thienopyridine prodrug that irreversibly blocks P2Y12 with more potent inhibition than clopidogrel. It carries a higher bleeding risk and is avoided in patients with prior stroke or TIA.
Ticagrelor is a non-thienopyridine that blocks P2Y12 directly and reversibly, without needing metabolic activation. Dyspnea is a characteristic side effect.
Ticlopidine is an older thienopyridine P2Y12 blocker now largely replaced. Its use was limited by serious hematologic effects, including neutropenia and TTP.

PLX-HEM-003.detail: In the classic laboratory model, the intrinsic pathway begins with contact activation: factor XII, prekallikrein, and high-molecular-weight kininogen interact on a negatively charged surface, which then activates factor XI. Factor XIa activates factor IX, and factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates factor X. Deficiency of any of these prolongs the aPTT, although prekallikrein, HMWK, and factor XII deficiencies do not cause bleeding. The extrinsic pathway (tissue factor and factor VII) is assessed by the PT instead.

A cofactor that anchors prekallikrein and factor XI to the activating surface during contact activation; deficiency prolongs aPTT without bleeding.
A vitamin K-dependent serine protease activated by factor XIa; deficiency causes hemophilia B.
The cofactor for factor IXa in the tenase complex that activates factor X; deficiency causes hemophilia A.

history.detail: In the classic laboratory model of coagulation, the intrinsic pathway begins with contact activation of factor XII, which activates XI, then IX, with factor VIII acting as a cofactor for IXa. This pathway is assessed by the aPTT, which is prolonged by deficiency of any of these factors. PLX-HEM-004.detail: Cold agglutinins are usually IgM autoantibodies that bind red cells at temperatures below core body temperature and activate complement, leading mainly to extravascular hemolysis and sometimes acrocyanosis. Secondary cold agglutinin syndrome can follow infections such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Epstein-Barr virus, or accompany B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia and CLL. This differs from primary cold agglutinin disease, and CLL more classically causes warm autoimmune hemolysis.
tileNotes: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is a cause of atypical (walking) pneumonia. It can trigger transient cold agglutinins, classically directed against the I antigen, causing hemolysis.
Epstein-Barr virus infection, the usual cause of infectious mononucleosis, can provoke cold-reactive antibodies, classically against the i antigen. Hemolysis is usually transient.
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma that produces monoclonal IgM. The IgM can act as a cold agglutinin, causing secondary cold agglutinin syndrome.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a clonal B-cell malignancy of mature lymphocytes. It more often causes warm autoimmune hemolysis, but it can also produce cold-reactive antibodies.

PLX-HEM-005.detail: Several drugs can trigger antibody-mediated destruction of red cells, typically with a positive direct antiglobulin test. Mechanisms differ: penicillin and cephalosporins can bind to red cells as haptens, cephalosporins and rifampin can form immune complexes, and methyldopa induces true autoantibodies resembling warm autoimmune hemolysis. Recognizing a temporal link to a new drug matters because stopping it is the key treatment.
tileNotes: Penicillin at high doses can coat red cell membranes and act as a hapten, so drug-specific IgG binds the cells. These antibody-coated cells are removed extravascularly.
Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics that can cause immune hemolysis by drug adsorption or immune-complex mechanisms. Some cases are severe.
Rifampin is an antituberculous antibiotic that can trigger immune-complex hemolysis. This mechanism tends to cause acute intravascular hemolysis, sometimes with kidney injury.
Methyldopa is an antihypertensive that can induce autoantibodies against red cell antigens, mimicking warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. A positive DAT is more common than overt hemolysis.

PLX-HEM-006.detail: G6PD generates NADPH, which keeps glutathione reduced so red cells can neutralize oxidants. When G6PD is deficient, oxidant drugs or infection overwhelm this defense, hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages remove pieces of the membrane, producing bite cells. Classic drug triggers include primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, and nitrofurantoin; fava beans and infection are non-drug triggers. Risk varies by drug, dose, and enzyme variant.
tileNotes: An 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial used against liver-stage Plasmodium vivax and ovale; G6PD testing is required before use because it can cause severe hemolysis.
Sulfa antibiotics such as sulfamethoxazole are oxidant drugs that can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
A urinary tract antibiotic with oxidant properties that can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Infection is the most common trigger, as activated phagocytes release oxidants during the inflammatory response.

PLX-HEM-007.detail: In G6PD deficiency, red cells cannot maintain enough reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic macrophages remove these inclusions, leaving bite cells, and hemolysis occurs in episodes after triggers. The gene is on the X chromosome, so males are mainly affected, though heterozygous females can be affected. Heinz bodies and bite cells can occur in other oxidant hemolysis, but together with the inheritance pattern they point to G6PD deficiency.
tileNotes: Heinz bodies are inclusions of denatured, precipitated hemoglobin inside red cells. They are seen with supravital stains such as crystal violet rather than routine smear stains.
Bite cells (degmacytes) are red cells that look as if a bite was taken from their edge. They form when splenic macrophages remove Heinz bodies.
Episodic oxidative hemolysis refers to bursts of red cell destruction after triggers such as infection, drugs or fava beans. Between episodes, patients are often well.
X-linked recessive inheritance means the gene lies on the X chromosome, so hemizygous males are mainly affected. Heterozygous females can also be affected, depending on X-inactivation.

PLX-HEM-008.detail: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually caused by defects in red cell membrane proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin or band 3. Loss of membrane produces small, dense spherical cells that are less deformable and are trapped and destroyed in the spleen. Increased MCHC and osmotic fragility support the diagnosis, and a negative direct antiglobulin test is the key discriminator from warm autoimmune hemolysis, which also produces spherocytes. EMA binding is a modern confirmatory test.
tileNotes: Spherocytes are small, round red cells that lack central pallor. In hereditary spherocytosis they result from membrane loss due to cytoskeletal protein defects.
Increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) reflects cells that are relatively dehydrated with less membrane for their hemoglobin content. It is a useful clue on routine blood counts.
Increased osmotic fragility means red cells lyse more readily in hypotonic saline. Spherocytes have little spare surface area to swell, so they burst sooner.
A negative direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test shows no antibody or complement on red cells. It rules against immune causes of spherocytes such as warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

PLX-HEM-009.detail: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria arises from an acquired somatic PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell, preventing synthesis of GPI anchors. Affected blood cells lack GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 and CD59, leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and a tendency to thrombosis, often in unusual veins. Not every patient has thrombosis or cytopenias, and diagnosis is by flow cytometry for loss of GPI-anchored proteins.
tileNotes: An acquired PIGA mutation is a somatic change in a stem cell that blocks GPI anchor synthesis. It is not inherited, even though the PIGA gene is on the X chromosome.

Alcohol, isoniazid, chloramphenicol and linezolid are recognized causes through different mechanisms: isoniazid antagonizes vitamin B6, whereas alcohol, chloramphenicol and linezolid impair mitochondrial function or protein synthesis. PLX-HEM-023.detail: Humans have four alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16, and in the classic deletion model, disease severity tracks the number lost. One deletion gives a silent carrier, two cause mild microcytic trait, three cause hemoglobin H disease, and four cause hemoglobin Bart hydrops fetalis. PLX-HEM-032.detail: Primary hemostasis is the formation of the initial platelet plug, which depends on platelet adhesion via von Willebrand factor, platelet aggregation, and an adequate number of circulating platelets. Defects at any of these steps classically cause mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding and menorrhagia, rather than the deep joint and muscle bleeds typical of coagulation factor deficiencies.
tileNotes: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an inherited deficiency of the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex, the receptor that binds von Willebrand factor. Platelets cannot adhere normally, and patients often have mild thrombocytopenia with large platelets.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an inherited deficiency of platelet GPIIb/IIIa, the receptor that links platelets together through fibrinogen. Adhesion is intact but aggregation fails, so the platelet plug cannot form properly.

In immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), autoantibodies coat platelets and shorten their survival through splenic clearance. Platelet function is normal, but the low count impairs plug formation and causes mucocutaneous bleeding.

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by low or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor. Impaired platelet adhesion causes mucosal bleeding, and reduced factor VIII can add a secondary hemostasis component.

PLX-HEM-033.detail: Treatment of immune thrombocytopenia aims to stop bleeding and raise the platelet count, either by reducing immune-mediated platelet destruction or by stimulating platelet production. Glucocorticoids, with or without IVIG, are typical first-line options, while rituximab and thrombopoietin-receptor agonists are usually second-line. The choice is individualized according to bleeding, severity and chronicity rather than following a fixed sequence.
tileNotes: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone or dexamethasone suppress the immune system broadly. In ITP they are a usual first-line treatment, reducing autoantibody-mediated platelet clearance.

IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) is pooled antibody from donors given intravenously. It is thought to work largely by blocking Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, and it can raise platelet counts quickly when a rapid response is needed.
Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 that depletes B cells. By reducing the cells that produce antiplatelet antibodies, it serves as a second-line option in ITP.

Thrombopoietin-receptor agonists such as romiplostim and eltrombopag stimulate megakaryocytes to make more platelets. Rather than reducing destruction, they boost production and are a second-line choice in ITP.

PLX-HEM-037.detail: Inherited thrombophilias are genetic conditions that tip the balance toward clotting, most often presenting as venous thromboembolism such as deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. They act by reducing natural anticoagulant activity, causing resistance to activated protein C, or raising prothrombin levels. Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, and protein S deficiency is another recognized cause.

PLX-HEM-040.detail: Overt disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) results from systemic activation of coagulation, often triggered by sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications or malignancy. Platelets and clotting factors are consumed while fibrin is formed and broken down, producing the classic pattern of low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer. Because fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant, it may be normal early, so trends over time matter.
tileNotes: Thrombocytopenia, a low platelet count, occurs in DIC because platelets are consumed in widespread microvascular clots. A falling count over time is a useful clue.
Both clotting times lengthen in DIC because coagulation factors are used up faster than they are replaced. Prolonged PT and aPTT together point to consumption across the common pathway.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin during clotting, so it falls as clotting is consumed in DIC. As an acute-phase reactant it may initially be normal or high, so a declining trend is informative.
D-dimer is a breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin. It rises in DIC because fibrin is continually formed and then lysed by plasmin.

PLX-HEM-043.detail: Psammoma bodies are round, concentrically laminated calcifications thought to form from dystrophic calcification of degenerating tumor cells, often in papillary architecture. The classic associated tumors are remembered with the mnemonic PSaMMoma: papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian carcinoma, meningioma and mesothelioma. They are common in the first three and less prominent in mesothelioma, so seeing them on histology or cytology narrows the differential.
tileNotes: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer. Psammoma bodies are a classic histologic feature, alongside papillae and nuclei with a cleared, ground-glass appearance (Orphan Annie eye nuclei).
A meningioma is a usually benign tumor arising from arachnoid cells of the meninges. Whorled cell arrangements that calcify into psammoma bodies are a characteristic microscopic finding.
Serous papillary ovarian carcinoma is a common malignant epithelial ovarian tumor. Its papillary projections frequently contain psammoma bodies.

Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor of the pleura or peritoneum strongly linked to asbestos exposure. Psammoma bodies can occur, particularly in the epithelioid type, though they are less prominent than in the other classic tumors.

Busulfan, cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are classic alkylating agents, while cisplatin is a platinum compound that crosslinks DNA in an alkylating-like way. Ifosfamide is a nitrogen mustard closely related to cyclophosphamide. It shares the risk of hemorrhagic cystitis and can also cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
Cisplatin is a platinum compound that forms DNA crosslinks, so it is described as alkylating-like rather than a classic alkylator. Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are its classic toxicities.

PLX-HEM-049.detail: Several chemotherapy drugs have well-known toxicities that can be reduced by a specific supportive agent. Mesna protects the bladder from cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide metabolites, dexrazoxane offers cardioprotection with anthracyclines, amifostine reduces selected cisplatin and radiation toxicity, and leucovorin rescues normal cells after high-dose methotrexate. These are targeted uses chosen for specific situations, not universal prophylaxis.
tileNotes: Mesna is a thiol compound that binds acrolein, a toxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide, in the urine. It is used to reduce the risk of hemorrhagic cystitis.
Dexrazoxane is an iron-chelating agent used to reduce anthracycline (for example doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity. It is thought to limit iron-dependent free radical damage to the heart.
Amifostine is a free radical scavenger used to reduce selected cisplatin toxicity, such as nephrotoxicity, and some radiation toxicity. It protects normal tissue in specific settings.
Leucovorin (folinic acid) is a reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase. It rescues normal cells after high-dose methotrexate and, separately, enhances the effect of 5-fluorouracil.

PLX-HEM-050.detail: Kinases add phosphate groups to proteins and act as switches in growth signaling pathways. When mutated, amplified or fused, these kinases become constitutively active and drive tumor growth, which makes them targets for drugs such as imatinib, vemurafenib, ruxolitinib and trastuzumab. Not all are receptor tyrosine kinases: HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase, BCR-ABL1 and JAK2 are non-receptor tyrosine kinases, and BRAF is a serine/threonine kinase.

JAK2 is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that transmits signals from cytokine receptors such as the erythropoietin receptor. The V617F mutation drives myeloproliferative neoplasms such as polycythemia vera.
HER2 (ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase in the EGFR family. Gene amplification occurs in a subset of breast and gastric cancers and is targeted by trastuzumab.

PLX-HEM-051.detail: Many lymphomas carry characteristic chromosomal translocations that place an oncogene next to an active regulatory element, often the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14, or create a fusion protein. Burkitt (MYC), follicular (BCL2), mantle cell (CCND1) and gastric MALT lymphoma (BIRC3-MALT1) are classic pairs. These translocations support diagnosis, but none is present in every case of its disease.
tileNotes: Burkitt lymphoma is a very aggressive B-cell lymphoma. Its classic translocation, t(8;14), places MYC next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, driving rapid cell proliferation.
Follicular lymphoma is an indolent B-cell lymphoma arising from germinal center cells. The t(14;18) translocation overexpresses BCL2, an anti-apoptotic protein that lets cells avoid programmed death.
Mantle cell lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma, often aggressive, arising from the mantle zone. Its t(11;14) translocation overexpresses cyclin D1 (CCND1), pushing cells through the cell cycle.
Gastric MALT lymphoma is a marginal zone lymphoma often linked to chronic H. pylori infection. The t(11;18) BIRC3-MALT1 fusion is its most frequent translocation, though present in only a subset.

Cold agglutinins are antibodies, usually IgM, that bind red cells at cool temperatures and cause agglutination or hemolysis. A monoclonal IgM in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia can have this activity in some patients.

PLX-HEM-065.detail: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs when large numbers of tumor cells break down, usually after starting treatment for a rapidly growing cancer such as a high-grade lymphoma or acute leukemia. Released potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (metabolized to uric acid) overwhelm renal excretion, and phosphate binds calcium, lowering serum calcium. The resulting abnormalities can cause arrhythmias and acute kidney injury, so prevention with hydration and urate-lowering drugs is standard in high-risk patients.

Hyperuricemia is an elevated serum uric acid level. Purines from released nucleic acids are metabolized to uric acid, which can precipitate in renal tubules; allopurinol or rasburicase are used to prevent or treat it.
Hypocalcemia is a low serum calcium level. In tumor lysis syndrome it is secondary to hyperphosphatemia, as phosphate binds and precipitates calcium, and it can cause tetany or arrhythmias.

PSY-001.detail: Defense mechanisms are largely unconscious mental processes that protect against anxiety or distressing emotions, and they are often ranked from immature to mature. Mature defenses handle conflict in healthy, socially adaptive ways while keeping contact with reality. Suppression is the notable exception that is a conscious choice; exam questions often ask learners to tell it apart from repression, which is unconscious.
tileNotes: Suppression is the deliberate, conscious decision to postpone attention to a distressing thought or feeling until a more suitable time. Unlike repression, the person remains aware of the issue.
Altruism means coping with distress by helping others in a way that brings personal satisfaction. An example is a person who lost a relative to cancer volunteering to support other families.
Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity. A classic example is redirecting aggressive urges into competitive sport.
Humor allows a person to acknowledge a painful or awkward situation by focusing on its amusing aspects. It eases tension without distorting the reality of what is happening.

PSY-002.detail: Operant conditioning, described by Skinner, is learning in which the consequences of a behavior change how often it occurs. Reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases it, while positive means a stimulus is added and negative means one is removed. Crossing these two dimensions gives four distinct consequence types, and exam questions often test the common confusion between negative reinforcement and punishment.
tileNotes: Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus after a behavior to make it more likely. For example, a child receives praise for finishing homework and does so more often.

Negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior, making the behavior more likely. Taking an analgesic that relieves a headache, and then using it again, is an example; it is not a form of punishment.
Positive punishment adds an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior to make it less likely. Scolding a child for running into the street is an example.
Negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus after a behavior to make it less likely. Taking away a teenager's phone after breaking curfew is an example.

PSY-019.detail: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway can cause several distinct movement disorders, collectively called extrapyramidal symptoms. Acute dystonia, parkinsonism and akathisia tend to appear earlier, while tardive dyskinesia develops after long-term exposure and may persist. Recognizing each matters because management differs, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a separate systemic emergency rather than one of these movement disorders.

Drug-induced parkinsonism produces bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor resembling Parkinson disease. It results from reduced dopamine signaling in the striatum and often improves with dose reduction or an anticholinergic.

Akathisia is a distressing inner restlessness with an urge to keep moving, such as pacing or shifting legs. It can be mistaken for worsening agitation, and beta-blockers such as propranolol are often used.
Tardive dyskinesia is involuntary, repetitive movements, often of the mouth, lips and tongue, after long-term dopamine blocker use. It can be persistent, and VMAT2 inhibitors are used in treatment.

PULM-002.detail: Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor strongly linked to smoking and to paraneoplastic syndromes. It can secrete hormones such as ADH and ACTH, and it can provoke antibodies that cross-react with neural targets, causing Lambert-Eaton syndrome or cerebellar degeneration. Chromogranin, synaptophysin and CD56 form the standard tissue staining panel, while neuron-specific enolase is mainly a serum marker with poor specificity on tissue. PULM-004.detail: Lobar pneumonia, classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, involves a large part of or an entire lobe. Pathologists describe four classic stages, from vascular congestion through red and gray hepatization to resolution. This is a classic pathological sequence rather than a fixed timeline, and different stages can coexist within the same lobe, especially in treated patients.
tileNotes: Congestion is the first stage, with engorged alveolar capillaries and alveoli containing edema fluid and many bacteria. The affected lung is heavy, red and boggy.
In red hepatization, alveoli fill with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin, giving the lobe a red, firm, liver-like consistency. The term hepatization refers to this resemblance to liver.
During gray hepatization, red cells break down while a fibrinosuppurative exudate persists. The lobe turns grayish-brown and remains firm and dry.
Resolution is enzymatic digestion of the exudate, which is then resorbed, coughed up or cleared by macrophages. Normal lung architecture is usually restored.

PULM-010.detail: Hypoxemia has five classic mechanisms: low inspired oxygen, hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, ventilation-perfusion mismatch and right-to-left shunt. Supplemental oxygen can improve the first four because extra oxygen reaches ventilated, perfused alveoli, whereas blood passing through a true shunt never contacts ventilated alveoli. Response to oxygen is a useful bedside clue, although improvement is not guaranteed and mixed shunt physiology blunts it.
tileNotes: Low inspired oxygen occurs at high altitude, where barometric pressure and therefore alveolar oxygen pressure fall. The A-a gradient is normal, and raising inspired oxygen corrects the hypoxemia.

Alveolar hypoventilation, as in opioid overdose or neuromuscular weakness, raises alveolar CO2 and lowers alveolar oxygen. The A-a gradient is normal, and supplemental oxygen improves oxygenation without fixing the hypercapnia.

In diffusion impairment, oxygen crosses a thickened or reduced alveolar-capillary membrane too slowly, as in interstitial lung disease. Raising alveolar oxygen increases the driving gradient and improves hypoxemia.

Ventilation-perfusion mismatch is an imbalance between airflow and blood flow across lung units, as in COPD, asthma or pulmonary embolism. It is the most common cause of hypoxemia and usually improves with supplemental oxygen.

PULM-011.detail: PaO2 measures oxygen dissolved in plasma, so it can be normal even when tissues are starved of oxygen. Anemia, carbon monoxide and methemoglobinemia reduce functional oxygen carriage by hemoglobin, while cyanide (and partly carbon monoxide) blocks mitochondrial use of oxygen. Recognizing this avoids false reassurance from a normal arterial blood gas.
tileNotes: Anemia is a reduced hemoglobin concentration. PaO2 and saturation stay normal, but total oxygen content and delivery fall because less hemoglobin is available to carry oxygen.

Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more avidly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and shifting the curve left. It also inhibits cytochrome oxidase, and standard pulse oximetry can read falsely normal.

Methemoglobinemia occurs when heme iron is oxidized to the ferric state, which cannot carry oxygen; triggers include dapsone, nitrites and benzocaine. Blood may look chocolate-brown while PaO2 remains normal.

Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, blocking mitochondrial oxygen use (histotoxic hypoxia) and causing lactic acidosis. Arterial oxygen content can be normal, and venous blood may stay unusually well oxygenated.

PULM-012.detail: ARDS is acute diffuse alveolar damage producing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and severe hypoxemia. Triggers may injure the lung directly, as with pneumonia and gastric acid aspiration, or indirectly through systemic inflammation, as with sepsis and acute pancreatitis. Classic signs are increased tactile fremitus, dullness, bronchial breath sounds over peripheral lung and crackles. The ejaculatory duct forms from the terminal mesonephric duct beyond the seminal vesicle and opens into the prostatic urethra.

REPRO-011.detail: Postpartum hemorrhage is grouped by the 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue and Thrombin. REPRO-024.detail: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency, most common in adolescents, in which rotation of the spermatic cord obstructs venous outflow and then arterial inflow. Testicular salvage is highest with detorsion within about 6 hours. The bell-clapper deformity, inadequate fixation of the testis to the tunica vaginalis, allows the testis to rotate and lie horizontally. Epididymitis is the main look-alike: onset is more gradual, the cremasteric reflex is usually preserved, pain may ease with elevation (Prehn sign), and Doppler flow is increased. Clinical suspicion should not be delayed for imaging, and partial torsion can show some flow.
tileNotes: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, reflects acute ischemia from cord twisting.
Shortening of the twisted cord pulls the testis up, and it often lies horizontally because of a bell-clapper deformity.
Stroking the inner thigh normally elevates the testis. The reflex is usually absent on the affected side in torsion.
Color Doppler ultrasound shows decreased or absent intratesticular blood flow. Normal flow does not exclude partial or intermittent torsion.

history.detail: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that cuts off testicular blood flow, making it a surgical emergency. A bell-clapper deformity often predisposes, and classic clues are sudden severe pain, a high-riding testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and reduced or absent flow on color Doppler. No finding is universal, preserved flow does not exclude torsion, and strong clinical suspicion should prompt surgery without waiting for imaging.
tileNotes: Torsion typically causes abrupt, severe unilateral testicular pain, often with nausea and vomiting. A sudden onset favors torsion over the more gradual pain of epididymitis.
A high-riding testis sits higher than normal, often with a horizontal lie, because the twisted cord shortens. The bell-clapper deformity, which lets the testis rotate freely, predisposes to torsion.
The cremasteric reflex is elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is stroked. Its absence is a classic sign of torsion, while a present reflex makes torsion less likely but does not exclude it.
Color Doppler ultrasound assesses blood flow within the testis. Reduced or absent flow supports torsion, but partial or intermittent torsion can show preserved flow.
