REPRO-025.detail: Acute bacterial epididymitis has two main patterns. In younger sexually active men it is usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas in older men or after instrumentation or catheterization, enteric gram-negatives such as Escherichia coli predominate, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in catheter-associated, instrumented or immunocompromised cases. Age and exposure history guide empiric antibiotic choice.
tileNotes: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium and a common sexually transmitted infection. It is a leading cause of epididymitis in younger sexually active men, sometimes with only mild urethritis.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that causes urethritis and other sexually transmitted infections. Ascending infection can cause epididymitis, so empiric treatment in younger men covers both gonorrhea and chlamydia.

Escherichia coli is a gram-negative enteric rod and the leading cause of urinary tract infections. It is the most common cause of epididymitis in older men, often with urinary obstruction or after instrumentation.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic gram-negative rod associated with healthcare exposure. It causes epididymitis mainly after catheterization or urologic instrumentation, or in immunocompromised patients.

CARD-053.detail: Each condition causes aortic regurgitation by stretching or tearing the aortic root, not by damaging the valve leaflets first. When the root and annulus widen, or a tear disrupts the commissures that hold the cusps, otherwise normal leaflets fail to close in diastole. This separates them from primary leaflet causes such as bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease, and endocarditis. Location matters: disease that spares the ascending aorta, such as an abdominal aortic aneurysm or a distal type B dissection, usually does not cause AR.
tileNotes: A tear in the aortic intima that lets blood split the media. A type A (ascending) dissection can extend into the root, strip support from the commissures, and let a cusp prolapse, producing a new diastolic murmur.

Dilation of the thoracic aorta, often from cystic medial degeneration, hypertension, or connective tissue disease. When the ascending aorta and root widen, the annulus stretches and the cusps can no longer meet.

Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) defects in Marfan syndrome weaken the aortic media, with dilation classically at the sinuses of Valsalva. The enlarging root pulls the cusps apart, and it can also progress to dissection.
Syphilitic aortitis causes endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, ischemic loss of the media, and a tree-bark intima. The resulting ascending aortic aneurysm dilates the root and causes AR.

DERM-004.detail: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is a toxin-mediated blistering disease, usually in infants and young children, in which circulating exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 and splits the epidermis high in the stratum granulosum. The superficial split gives widespread fragile skin with a positive Nikolsky sign, while mucosa is spared. Toxic epidermal necrolysis instead causes full-thickness necrosis with mucosal involvement, and pemphigus vulgaris is autoimmune against desmoglein 3 with oral lesions. Bullous impetigo shares the same toxin and split but stays localized.
tileNotes: Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins A and B are serine proteases released at a distant focus of infection. They spread through the blood, which is why the skin peeling is widespread even though the skin itself is often sterile.
The toxin cuts desmoglein 1, the main adhesion protein in the upper epidermis. Losing it separates cells within the stratum granulosum, so blisters are very superficial and heal without scarring.

Gentle lateral pressure shears off the upper epidermis because the toxin has broken cell to cell adhesion throughout the skin. A generalized positive Nikolsky sign distinguishes SSSS from localized bullous impetigo.
Mucosa relies mainly on desmoglein 3, which the toxin does not cleave, so the mouth and eyes are spared. Mucosal involvement points instead toward toxic epidermal necrolysis or pemphigus vulgaris.

MSK-006.detail: These findings point to calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) deposition, which causes pseudogout, most often in the knee or wrist of older adults. Synovial fluid shows rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent and look blue when parallel to the compensator. Gout is the look-alike: monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, and yellow when parallel. Chondrocalcinosis supports CPPD but is not required. CPPD is associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia.
tileNotes: CPP crystals are short, blunt, rhomboid or rod shapes in synovial fluid, often inside neutrophils. Gout crystals, by contrast, are long and needle-shaped.

Under polarized light CPP crystals appear only faintly bright, and their birefringence is positive, so they look blue when parallel to the compensator. Urate crystals in gout are brightly and negatively birefringent.

Calcification of cartilage seen on x-ray, classically in the knee menisci or the wrist triangular fibrocartilage. It supports CPPD but can be absent in acute pseudogout and also occurs without symptoms.

The visible result of positive birefringence under a red compensator: CPP crystals look blue when their long axis is parallel to the slow axis and yellow when perpendicular. Urate crystals show the reverse.
